subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: The King-Byng Affair of 1926 and the Constitutional Crisis
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: the King-Byng Affair was a 1926 constitutional crisis in which Governor General Lord Byng refused Prime Minister Mackenzie Kings request to dissolve Parliament, raising lasting questions about the proper limits of the Governor Generals discretionary power in Canadian government.

quiz.q: Who were the two main figures involved in the King-Byng Affair?
options: Prime Minister Mackenzie King and Governor General Lord Byng
Prime Minister Lester Pearson and a provincial premier
Prime Minister John A. Macdonald and Queen Victoria
Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau and a foreign ambassador

quiz.q: What did Governor General Byng refuse to do in 1926?
options: Call a referendum on Confederation
Approve the Balfour Declaration
Dissolve Parliament at Prime Minister Kings request
Sign the Treaty of Versailles

quiz.q: What broader constitutional question did the King-Byng Affair raise?
options: Whether Canada should adopt a new flag
The proper limits of the Governor Generals discretionary power
Whether Quebec should separate from Canada
Whether Newfoundland should join Confederation

quiz.q: In what year did the King-Byng Affair occur?
The King-Byng Affair is often discussed alongside which other 1926 milestone in Canadian constitutional history?
options: The Naval Service Act
The Nisgaa Treaty
The St. Lawrence Seaway
The Balfour Declaration

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Writing: The Eulogy and Commemorative Writing
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: a eulogy is a speech or piece of writing that honours and remembers a person, typically highlighting their character, achievements, and impact on others, and commemorative writing more broadly uses a respectful, reflective tone to mark significant people or events.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a eulogy?
options: To criticize a persons flaws in detail
To honour and remember a person by highlighting their character and impact
To entertain an audience with unrelated humour only
To provide a strictly factual biography with no reflection

quiz.q: What tone does commemorative writing typically use?
options: A purely technical and clinical tone
A sarcastic and dismissive tone
An angry and confrontational tone
A respectful and reflective tone

quiz.q: Which detail would most likely appear in a well-written eulogy?
options: An unrelated list of statistics
A detailed critique of the persons career failures
A specific memory that illustrates the persons kindness or character
A summary of unrelated current events

quiz.q: Why do eulogies often include anecdotes?
options: Anecdotes are required by law in formal speeches
Anecdotes bring a persons character to life for the audience
Anecdotes replace the need for any structure
Anecdotes are only used in fictional writing

quiz.q: Commemorative writing can also be used to mark ___.
options: Only failures and setbacks
Significant historical events or achievements, not just individuals
Only birthdays with no other occasions
Nothing beyond a single specific person

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Statistics: An Introduction to Hypothesis Testing
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: hypothesis testing is a statistical method for evaluating whether observed data provides enough evidence to reject a null hypothesis, a default assumption of no effect or no difference, in favour of an alternative hypothesis.

quiz.q: What is a null hypothesis?
options: A statement with no statistical meaning
A hypothesis with no possible outcome
A hypothesis that is always proven true
A default assumption of no effect or no difference

quiz.q: What does hypothesis testing evaluate?
options: Whether a graph is drawn correctly
Whether observed data provides enough evidence to reject the null hypothesis
Whether a number is even or odd
Whether an equation has a solution

quiz.q: What is the alternative hypothesis?
options: A hypothesis with no relationship to the null hypothesis
A hypothesis used only in geometry
The hypothesis proposing that an effect or difference does exist
A hypothesis identical to the null hypothesis in every case

quiz.q: Why is hypothesis testing important in statistics?
options: It guarantees results with complete certainty every time
It eliminates the need for any data collection
It provides a structured method for making inferences from sample data
It only applies to whole numbers

quiz.q: A low p-value in hypothesis testing typically suggests ___.
options: That no data was collected
That the null hypothesis is definitely true
That the experiment must be repeated exactly
Stronger evidence against the null hypothesis

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Earth Science: Glaciers and Ice Ages
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand: glaciers are large, slow-moving masses of ice formed by the accumulation and compaction of snow over long periods, and ice ages are extended periods of global cooling during which glaciers expand significantly, reshaping landscapes through erosion and deposition.

quiz.q: How do glaciers form?
options: Through the accumulation and compaction of snow over long periods
Through rapid evaporation of ocean water
Through sudden flooding events
Through volcanic eruptions releasing ash

quiz.q: What is an ice age?
options: A brief period of extreme heat with no ice
An extended period of global cooling during which glaciers expand significantly
A single day of unusually cold weather
A period when all ice on Earth melts completely

quiz.q: How do glaciers reshape landscapes?
options: Glaciers have no effect on landscapes
Through processes of erosion and deposition as they move
Only through volcanic activity
Only by melting instantly with no movement

quiz.q: What landform is commonly created by glacial deposition?
options: A coral reef formed underwater
A volcano formed from lava
A moraine, a ridge of accumulated debris
A sand dune formed only by wind

quiz.q: Glaciers are classified as which type of natural feature due to their movement?
options: Slow-moving masses of ice
Stationary rock formations with no movement
Fast-flowing liquid water bodies
Gas clouds in the atmosphere

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: The Manitoba Act of 1870 and the Creation of Manitoba
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: the Manitoba Act of 1870 created Canadas fifth province following the Red River Resistance led by Louis Riel, establishing provisions for bilingual government services and land grants for the Metis population of the Red River Settlement.

quiz.q: What did the Manitoba Act of 1870 create?
options: The Northwest Territories
The province of Saskatchewan
The province of Alberta
The province of Manitoba

quiz.q: What event preceded and influenced the Manitoba Act?
options: The Halifax Explosion
The Klondike Gold Rush
The Battle of Vimy Ridge
The Red River Resistance led by Louis Riel

quiz.q: What number province did Manitoba become?
options: The fifth province
The second province
The first province
The tenth province

quiz.q: What did the Manitoba Act include provisions for?
options: An immediate declaration of independence from Canada
The complete removal of French language rights
Bilingual government services and land grants for the Metis population
The abolition of all provincial governments

quiz.q: In what year was the Manitoba Act passed?

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Grammar: Nominalization and Concise Writing
subjects.summary: Grade 8 Writing strand: nominalization turns verbs or adjectives into nouns (decide becomes decision), which can sometimes make writing wordier, so concise writing often favours strong, direct verbs instead.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Grammar: Nominalization and Concise Writing

quiz.q: Nominalization refers to ___.
options: Turning a noun into a verb
A rule unrelated to word forms
Removing all nouns from a sentence
Turning a verb or adjective into a noun

quiz.q: Which is an example of a nominalized form of the verb decide?
options: Undecided
Decide
Decision
Deciding quickly

quiz.q: Why might overusing nominalizations make writing less concise?
options: Nominalized words have no effect on sentence length
Nominalization always makes writing shorter and clearer
Concise writing always requires more nominalizations
It can replace strong, direct verbs with wordier noun phrases

quiz.q: Which sentence demonstrates more concise, direct writing?
options: A decision was made by her quickly.
The making of a decision occurred quickly by her.
She made a decision quickly.
She decided quickly.

quiz.q: Why might a writer choose to revise nominalized sentences into more direct ones?
options: Revising sentences has no effect on writing quality
Direct sentences with strong verbs are often clearer and more engaging
Concise writing has no connection to verb choice
Nominalized sentences are always clearer than direct ones

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Algebra: Partial Fraction Decomposition
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: partial fraction decomposition rewrites a complex rational expression as a sum of simpler fractions with lower-degree denominators, a technique useful for simplifying expressions and preparing them for further operations like integration.

quiz.q: What does partial fraction decomposition do?
options: Removes all variables from an expression
Converts a fraction into a whole number only
Rewrites a complex rational expression as a sum of simpler fractions
Combines several fractions into one complicated fraction

quiz.q: What kind of denominators do the resulting simpler fractions have?
options: Denominators equal to zero
No denominators at all
Denominators of infinitely high degree
Lower-degree denominators than the original expression

quiz.q: Partial fraction decomposition is especially useful in preparing expressions for ___.
options: Only basic addition of whole numbers
Simple counting with no further use
Further operations such as integration
Removing all fractions from mathematics permanently

quiz.q: What must be true about a rational expressions degree before typical partial fraction decomposition is applied?
options: The numerators degree should be less than the denominators degree
The expression must have no numerator
The denominator must always be a single variable
The numerator must always equal zero

quiz.q: Why might a mathematician decompose a complex fraction into partial fractions?
options: To convert the expression into a whole number only
To eliminate all mathematical meaning from the expression
To make the expression easier to analyze, simplify, or integrate
To make the expression permanently unsolvable

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: The Integumentary System: Skin, Hair, and Nails
subjects.summary: Grade 8 Science strand: the integumentary system, made up of skin, hair, and nails, protects the body from injury and infection, regulates temperature, and provides sensory information.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: The Integumentary System: Skin, Hair, and Nails

quiz.q: What organs make up the integumentary system?
options: The stomach and intestines
The brain and spinal cord
Skin, hair, and nails
The heart and lungs

quiz.q: What is one major function of the skin?
options: Digesting food
Pumping blood throughout the body
Producing sound
Protecting the body from injury and infection

quiz.q: How does the integumentary system help regulate body temperature?
options: By filtering air in the lungs
Through sweating and blood vessel changes near the skins surface
By producing digestive enzymes
It has no role in temperature regulation

quiz.q: What sensory information can skin provide?
options: Balance only
Taste only
Sound only
Touch, pressure, and temperature

quiz.q: Why is the integumentary system considered the bodys largest organ system?
options: It has no measurable size
It is smaller than a single cell
Skin covers the entire external surface of the body
It is located only in one small area

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: The Canadian Pacific Railway and National Unity
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: completed in 1885, the Canadian Pacific Railway fulfilled a promise made to British Columbia upon joining Confederation, linking the country from coast to coast and playing a central role in national unity, western settlement, and economic development.

quiz.q: What promise did the Canadian Pacific Railway fulfill?
options: A promise made to British Columbia upon joining Confederation
A promise made to Newfoundland in 1949
A promise made to Quebec after the 1867 Confederation
A promise made during the War of 1812

quiz.q: In what year was the Canadian Pacific Railway completed?
What role did the railway play in Canadian development?
options: It linked the country from coast to coast and supported western settlement
It disconnected eastern and western Canada
It was used only for local city transportation
It had no effect on national development

quiz.q: The construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway is often linked to which controversial labour practice?
options: The use of only unionized labour with full benefits
The use of underpaid Chinese labourers under dangerous conditions
The exclusive use of volunteer labour with no pay disputes
A complete ban on all immigrant labour

quiz.q: Why is the Canadian Pacific Railway considered significant to national unity?
options: It only served military purposes
It separated the provinces into isolated regions
It had no connection to economic development
It physically and economically connected the provinces of a vast country

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Media Literacy: Algorithmic Bias and Filter Bubbles
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: recommendation algorithms on social media and search platforms personalize content based on past behaviour, which can create filter bubbles that reinforce existing beliefs and limit exposure to diverse perspectives, an important concern in media literacy.

quiz.q: What is a filter bubble?
options: A physical device used to filter internet traffic
A type of formal essay structure
A state in which personalized algorithms limit exposure to diverse perspectives
A method of fact-checking news articles

quiz.q: How do recommendation algorithms typically personalize content?
options: By analyzing a users past behaviour and preferences
By randomly selecting content with no pattern
By ignoring user activity entirely
By showing every user identical content

quiz.q: Why are filter bubbles a concern in media literacy?
options: They eliminate the need for critical thinking entirely
They can reinforce existing beliefs and reduce exposure to differing viewpoints
They have no effect on how people understand issues
They guarantee complete objectivity in all content

quiz.q: What term describes systematic unfairness in how an algorithm ranks or recommends content?
options: Algorithmic redundancy
Algorithmic neutrality
Algorithmic transparency
Algorithmic bias

quiz.q: What is one strategy for countering the effects of filter bubbles?
options: Avoiding all forms of media entirely
Sharing content without reading it first
Only using a single platform for all information
Deliberately seeking out sources with differing perspectives

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Geometry: An Introduction to Non-Euclidean Geometry
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: non-Euclidean geometry explores geometric systems that reject Euclids parallel postulate, including spherical and hyperbolic geometry, revealing that the familiar rules of flat-plane geometry are not the only consistent geometric framework.

quiz.q: What does non-Euclidean geometry reject?
options: The existence of angles
The concept of a triangle entirely
All numerical measurement
Euclids parallel postulate

quiz.q: What are two major types of non-Euclidean geometry?
options: Spherical and hyperbolic geometry
Rational and irrational geometry
Positive and negative geometry
Linear and quadratic geometry

quiz.q: In spherical geometry, what happens to the sum of a triangles interior angles?
options: It is always less than 90 degrees
It equals zero degrees
It is greater than 180 degrees
It always equals exactly 180 degrees

quiz.q: Why is non-Euclidean geometry significant in mathematics?
options: It disproves the existence of shapes entirely
It has no real mathematical applications
It proves that all geometry is invalid
It shows that flat-plane geometry is not the only consistent geometric system

quiz.q: Non-Euclidean geometry has important applications in which modern scientific field?
options: General relativity and the study of curved spacetime
Basic arithmetic only
Elementary counting techniques
Simple linear equations only

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Biology: Coral Reefs and Marine Ecosystems
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand: coral reefs are diverse marine ecosystems built by colonies of tiny animals called coral polyps, which form calcium carbonate skeletons that provide habitat for a vast range of marine species, though reefs remain highly sensitive to changes in ocean temperature and acidity.

quiz.q: What are coral reefs built by?
options: Deep-sea plant colonies
Large solitary fish
Deposits of volcanic ash
Colonies of tiny animals called coral polyps

quiz.q: What do coral polyps produce that forms the structure of a reef?
options: Pure oxygen gas only
Calcium carbonate skeletons
Layers of ice
Large deposits of sand with no structure

quiz.q: Why are coral reefs ecologically important?
options: They only support a single species of fish
They provide habitat for a vast range of marine species
They have no effect on marine biodiversity
They exist only in freshwater lakes

quiz.q: What environmental change can cause coral bleaching?
options: Rising ocean temperatures
A drop in atmospheric pressure only
A decrease in ocean salinity to zero
An increase in the number of coral polyps

quiz.q: In addition to temperature, what other ocean condition threatens coral reef health?
options: Decreasing sunlight in deep trenches only
Increasing ocean acidity
Increasing freshwater rainfall only
Increasing oxygen levels only

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: The Rowell-Sirois Commission and Canadian Federalism
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: established in the late 1930s during the Great Depression, the Rowell-Sirois Commission examined the financial relationship between the federal and provincial governments, recommending reforms that reshaped Canadian federalism and expanded the federal governments role in social welfare.

quiz.q: When was the Rowell-Sirois Commission established?
options: In the late 1930s, during the Great Depression
Immediately after Confederation in 1867
After World War II in the 1950s
In the early 1800s

quiz.q: What relationship did the Rowell-Sirois Commission examine?
options: The relationship between Canada and the United Nations
The relationship between Canada and Britain only
The financial relationship between federal and provincial governments
The relationship between two rival political parties

quiz.q: What broader system did the commissions recommendations help reshape?
options: The Canadian electoral map only
International trade agreements with Europe
Canadian federalism
The structure of the British monarchy

quiz.q: What government role expanded as a result of related reforms?
options: The federal governments role in social welfare
The judicial branchs role in taxation only
The municipal governments role in defence
The provincial governments role in foreign policy

quiz.q: The Rowell-Sirois Commission was formed in response to economic difficulties caused by ___.
options: The 1918-1920 Spanish Flu Pandemic
The Great Depression
The Klondike Gold Rush
World War I

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Reading: Analyzing Pathetic Fallacy and Personification
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: pathetic fallacy attributes human emotions to nature or the weather to mirror a characters mood, while personification more broadly gives human qualities to any nonhuman thing, and both devices deepen atmosphere and symbolic meaning in a text.

quiz.q: What is pathetic fallacy?
options: Attributing human emotions to nature or weather to reflect a characters mood
A method of citing sources
A type of grammatical mistake
A logical error in an argument

quiz.q: What is personification?
options: Exaggerating a statement for emphasis
Giving human qualities to a nonhuman thing
Comparing two unlike things using like or as
Repeating a consonant sound for effect

quiz.q: Which sentence is an example of pathetic fallacy?
options: The weather forecast predicted rain for Tuesday.
The storm produced 50 millimetres of rainfall in one hour.
The character felt sad after losing the competition.
The angry storm clouds gathered as the heros despair deepened.

quiz.q: Why might an author use pathetic fallacy?
options: To remove emotional tone from a scene
To mirror and intensify a characters emotional state through the natural environment
To provide purely scientific weather data
To avoid describing any setting

quiz.q: How does personification typically deepen a text?
options: By replacing all characters with objects
By creating vivid imagery and symbolic meaning through humanlike nonhuman elements
By eliminating the need for description
By making a text purely literal with no symbolism

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Discrete Math: The Principle of Mathematical Induction
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: mathematical induction is a proof technique used to establish that a statement holds true for every natural number by proving a base case and then showing that if the statement holds for one case, it must hold for the next.

quiz.q: What does the principle of mathematical induction prove?
options: That a statement holds true for every natural number
That a statement is true for only one specific number
That a shape has a certain area
That an equation has no solution

quiz.q: What are the two main steps in a proof by induction?
options: Guessing the answer and checking with a calculator
Drawing a graph and measuring it
Listing every natural number individually
Proving a base case and proving the inductive step

quiz.q: What is the inductive step in a proof by induction?
options: Proving the statement is false for every case
Proving the statement only for the number one
Showing that if the statement holds for one case, it must hold for the next
Skipping directly to the conclusion with no justification

quiz.q: Why is proving only the base case not sufficient for induction?
options: A single case can never be part of a proof
The statement must also be shown to hold for all subsequent cases
The base case alone always proves a statement for every number
Induction requires no base case at all

quiz.q: Mathematical induction is especially useful for proving statements about ___.
options: Only geometric shapes with no numbers
Only continuous, non-integer measurements
Sequences, sums, and other statements indexed by natural numbers
Only statements with no variables

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Earth Science: Fossil Formation and the Geologic Time Scale
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand: fossils form when the remains or traces of organisms are preserved in sediment over long periods, and scientists use fossils alongside rock layers to construct the geologic time scale, a framework dividing Earths history into eras, periods, and epochs.

quiz.q: How do most fossils typically form?
options: Organisms instantly turn to stone upon death
Fossils are created by volcanic eruptions exclusively
Fossils form only within a single day
Remains or traces of organisms are preserved in sediment over long periods

quiz.q: What do scientists use fossils and rock layers to construct?
options: A weather forecasting model
A map of ocean currents
A periodic table of elements
The geologic time scale

quiz.q: What is the geologic time scale used for?
options: Measuring the temperature of the ocean
Calculating the speed of tectonic plates only
Predicting daily weather patterns
Dividing Earths history into eras, periods, and epochs

quiz.q: Why are fossils useful to scientists studying Earths history?
options: Fossils are unrelated to the study of evolution
Fossils only exist in modern rock layers
Fossils provide no useful scientific information
They provide evidence of past life forms and environmental conditions

quiz.q: What principle helps scientists determine the relative age of fossils in undisturbed rock layers?
options: Deeper layers are generally older than layers above them
Rock layer position has no relation to age
All rock layers are exactly the same age
Fossils in higher layers are always older

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: The Manitoba Schools Question and Language Rights
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: the Manitoba Schools Question was a major political controversy of the 1890s over the provinces decision to eliminate public funding for Catholic and French-language schools, a dispute that intensified debates over minority language rights across Canada.

quiz.q: What was the Manitoba Schools Question primarily about?
options: The elimination of public funding for Catholic and French-language schools
A disagreement over railway construction routes
A dispute over provincial boundaries
A conflict over agricultural land grants

quiz.q: In what decade did the Manitoba Schools Question arise?
options: The 1940s
The 1860s
The 1980s
The 1890s

quiz.q: What broader issue did the controversy intensify debate over?
options: Canadas naval policy
Immigration quotas from Europe
Minority language rights across Canada
Canadian participation in the League of Nations

quiz.q: Which two groups were most directly affected by the funding changes?
options: Catholic and Francophone communities in Manitoba
Protestant communities in British Columbia
Indigenous communities in the Arctic
English-speaking communities in Ontario

quiz.q: Why is the Manitoba Schools Question still studied today?
options: It illustrates long-standing tensions over language and religious rights in Canadian federalism
It only affected a single small town with no wider relevance
It was resolved with no controversy at the time
It had no lasting effect on Canadian politics

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Writing: The Investigative Report
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: an investigative report presents research findings on a specific issue through a clear structure, evidence-based analysis, and credible sourcing, aiming to inform readers and often to expose a problem or hold a subject accountable.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of an investigative report?
options: To present research findings on an issue through evidence-based analysis
To entertain readers with fictional events
To advertise a product or service
To express purely personal opinions with no evidence

quiz.q: What is essential to an effective investigative report?
options: A complete absence of structure
Unverified rumours presented as fact
Exclusively anonymous, unconfirmed claims
Credible sourcing and evidence-based analysis

quiz.q: Investigative reports often aim to ___.
options: Expose a problem or hold a subject accountable
Ignore public interest entirely
Promote a single product exclusively
Avoid any conclusions or findings

quiz.q: Which is a key step in producing an investigative report?
options: Skipping any fact-checking process
Gathering and verifying evidence from multiple credible sources
Relying on a single unverified source
Writing the conclusion before any research begins

quiz.q: Why is clear structure important in an investigative report?
options: Investigative reports should avoid any organization
Structure has no impact on how readers understand a report
Structure only matters in fictional writing
It helps readers follow the evidence and understand the findings logically

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Vectors: Scalar and Vector Projections
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: the scalar projection of one vector onto another measures how much of the first vector points in the direction of the second, while the vector projection expresses that amount as a vector itself, both calculated using the dot product.

quiz.q: What does a scalar projection measure?
options: The angle between two lines only
The number of dimensions in a vector space
The total area between two vectors
How much of one vector points in the direction of another

quiz.q: How does a vector projection differ from a scalar projection?
options: A vector projection has no direction at all
A vector projection is always equal to zero
A vector projection expresses the projected amount as a vector, not just a magnitude
A vector projection ignores the direction of the original vector

quiz.q: What operation is used to calculate a projection between two vectors?
options: The dot product
Division of the vectors magnitudes
The cross product only
Simple addition of the vectors

quiz.q: If two vectors are perpendicular, what is the scalar projection of one onto the other?
options: Equal to the magnitude of the longer vector
Always a negative number
Zero
Undefined in every case

quiz.q: Vector projections are useful in physics for calculating ___.
options: The component of a force acting in a specific direction
The total colour of an object
The taste of a substance
The temperature of a system

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Biology: Animal Behaviour, Instinct and Learning
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand: animal behaviour includes both instinctive actions, inherited and performed correctly without prior experience, and learned behaviours acquired through experience or observation, and understanding the balance between the two helps explain how species survive and adapt.

quiz.q: What is instinctive behaviour?
options: A random, meaningless action with no purpose
An inherited behaviour performed correctly without prior experience
A behaviour that must always be taught by a parent
A behaviour found only in plants

quiz.q: What is learned behaviour?
options: A behaviour that never changes throughout an animals life
A behaviour unrelated to survival
A behaviour acquired through experience or observation
A behaviour present at birth with no experience needed

quiz.q: Which of these is an example of instinctive behaviour?
options: A newborn sea turtle moving toward the ocean immediately after hatching
A bird learning a new song by mimicking another bird
A dog learning to sit after repeated training
A chimpanzee learning to use a tool after watching others

quiz.q: Why is learned behaviour advantageous for some species?
options: It has no effect on an animals survival
It allows animals to adapt their actions based on changing circumstances
It is identical to instinctive behaviour in every way
It prevents animals from ever adapting to their environment

quiz.q: Understanding the balance between instinct and learning helps scientists explain ___.
options: Only the diet of a single species
Only the physical appearance of animals
How different species survive and adapt to their environments
Nothing related to animal survival

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: British Columbia Joins Confederation in 1871
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: British Columbia joined Confederation in 1871 after negotiating key conditions with the federal government, most notably a promise to build a transcontinental railway connecting the province to the rest of Canada within ten years.

quiz.q: In what year did British Columbia join Confederation?
What major condition did British Columbia negotiate for joining Confederation?
options: A promise to build a transcontinental railway within ten years
A promise to remain a British colony forever
A permanent exemption from federal taxes
A guarantee of complete independence from Canada

quiz.q: What number province did British Columbia become upon joining?
options: The first province
The sixth province
The tenth province
The third province

quiz.q: Which railway project fulfilled the promise made to British Columbia?
options: The Grand Trunk Railway exclusively
The Canadian Pacific Railway
The St. Lawrence Seaway
The Trans-Canada Highway

quiz.q: Why was British Columbias entry into Confederation significant for Canada?
options: It had no effect on Canadas geographic extent
It caused Canada to lose access to the Pacific Ocean
It extended Canadian territory to the Pacific coast
It marked the end of Confederation expansion permanently

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Grammar: Appositives and Nonrestrictive Clauses
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: an appositive renames or explains a nearby noun, and a nonrestrictive clause adds extra, non-essential information about a noun, both typically set off with commas since removing them would not change the sentences essential meaning.

quiz.q: What does an appositive do?
options: Functions only as a preposition
Replaces a verb with a noun
Renames or explains a nearby noun
Introduces a question

quiz.q: What is a nonrestrictive clause?
options: A clause that adds extra, non-essential information about a noun
A clause with no grammatical function at all
A clause that functions as the main verb
A clause that is essential to identifying the noun it modifies

quiz.q: How are appositives and nonrestrictive clauses typically punctuated?
options: They are set off with exclamation marks
They always end with a question mark
They are set off with commas
They are never punctuated in any way

quiz.q: Which sentence contains an appositive?
options: My teacher inspires the class every single day.
My teacher, a former Olympic athlete, inspired the class.
My teacher inspired the class.
The teacher who inspired the class was an athlete.

quiz.q: Why can a nonrestrictive clause be removed without changing a sentences essential meaning?
options: Because it provides supplementary rather than identifying information
Because it is always the main clause of the sentence
Because nonrestrictive clauses never contain any information
Because removing any clause never changes meaning

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Probability: An Introduction to Bayes Theorem
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: Bayes Theorem provides a method for updating the probability of an event based on new evidence, relating conditional probabilities to revise an initial estimate into a more accurate one as additional information becomes available.

quiz.q: What does Bayes Theorem allow you to do?
options: Update the probability of an event based on new evidence
Solve a quadratic equation
Find the derivative of a function
Calculate the area of a triangle

quiz.q: Bayes Theorem relates which type of probabilities?
options: Only impossible events with probability zero
Only probabilities equal to exactly one
Only probabilities involving whole numbers
Conditional probabilities

quiz.q: What is the initial estimate of a probability, before new evidence is considered, often called?
options: The impossible probability
The irrelevant probability
The prior probability
The final probability

quiz.q: Why is Bayes Theorem useful in real-world decision-making?
options: It eliminates the need for any evidence
It allows estimates to be revised as new, relevant information becomes available
It only applies to events that never happen
It guarantees a certain outcome with no uncertainty

quiz.q: Bayes Theorem is widely applied in fields such as ___.
options: Only ancient historical record-keeping
Only measuring physical distances
Medical diagnosis and spam email filtering
Only basic arithmetic with whole numbers

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Chemistry: The Maillard Reaction and the Chemistry of Cooking
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand: the Maillard reaction is a chemical reaction between amino acids and reducing sugars that occurs when food is heated, producing the browning, aroma, and flavour changes seen in foods like toasted bread, seared meat, and roasted coffee.

quiz.q: What two components react in the Maillard reaction?
options: Only oxygen and carbon dioxide
Only fats and proteins with no sugars involved
Amino acids and reducing sugars
Only water and salt

quiz.q: What triggers the Maillard reaction in food?
options: Adding only cold water
Heat
Freezing temperatures
Complete darkness with no heat

quiz.q: What visible change does the Maillard reaction typically cause in food?
options: The food becomes completely transparent
Browning of the surface
The food loses all mass instantly
The food turns permanently blue

quiz.q: Which of these foods commonly shows the effects of the Maillard reaction?
options: Seared meat
Ice water
Uncooked rice grains
Raw lettuce

quiz.q: Besides browning, what other sensory changes does the Maillard reaction produce?
options: A permanent change in the foods temperature only
A complete loss of all smell and taste
An increase in the foods transparency only
Changes in aroma and flavour

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: Prince Edward Island Joins Confederation in 1873
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: Prince Edward Island joined Confederation in 1873, six years after the original union, after federal financial assistance helped resolve a long-standing land ownership dispute involving absentee landlords on the island.

quiz.q: In what year did Prince Edward Island join Confederation?
What long-standing dispute affected Prince Edward Island before Confederation?
options: A land ownership dispute involving absentee landlords
A dispute over provincial borders with Quebec
A disagreement over railway routes through the island
A conflict over fishing rights with the United States

quiz.q: What helped resolve the land dispute and encourage Confederation?
options: A treaty with the United States
A military intervention by Britain
A decision by the League of Nations
Federal financial assistance

quiz.q: How many years after the original 1867 Confederation did Prince Edward Island join?
options: Twenty years
Six years
Fifty years
One year

quiz.q: What number province did Prince Edward Island become?
options: The first province
The seventh province
The third province
The tenth province

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Literature: The Trickster Figure in Folklore and Fiction
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: the trickster is a recurring archetype found across many cultures mythologies and folklore, a clever, boundary-crossing figure who uses wit and deception to challenge authority, expose hypocrisy, or bring about change.

quiz.q: What defines a trickster figure?
options: A clever, boundary-crossing character who uses wit and deception
A character who always follows every rule strictly
A minor character who never affects the plot
A character with no personality traits

quiz.q: What role does a trickster often play in a narrative?
options: Remaining entirely passive throughout the story
Challenging authority or exposing hypocrisy through cunning
Enforcing strict order with no disruption
Narrating events with no involvement in the plot

quiz.q: Trickster figures appear in ___.
options: Only modern fiction with no historical roots
Only nonfiction historical writing
Many different cultures mythologies and folklore traditions
Only a single specific culture with no other examples

quiz.q: Which quality is most closely associated with trickster characters?
options: Complete honesty in every situation
A total lack of intelligence
Wit and cunning used to outsmart others
An inability to speak or communicate

quiz.q: Why do trickster figures often bring about change in a story?
options: Their disruptive, boundary-crossing actions challenge the existing order
They are always removed from the plot immediately
They have no influence on other characters
They strictly maintain the status quo at all times

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Complex Numbers: Roots of Unity
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: the nth roots of unity are the complex solutions to the equation z^n = 1, evenly spaced points on the unit circle in the complex plane that can be found using De Moivres Theorem and reveal deep connections between algebra and geometry.

quiz.q: What equation defines the nth roots of unity?
options: z^n = 0
z^n = 1
z + n = 1
z^n = n

quiz.q: Where are the nth roots of unity located in the complex plane?
options: Only at the origin
Only on the real number line
Evenly spaced points on the unit circle
Randomly scattered points with no pattern

quiz.q: Which earlier theorem is used to find the roots of unity?
options: De Moivres Theorem
The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
The Binomial Theorem
The Pythagorean Theorem

quiz.q: How many distinct nth roots of unity exist for a given positive integer n?
options: Exactly one, regardless of n
Exactly n
Infinitely many for every value of n
Exactly zero

quiz.q: The roots of unity reveal a connection between which two branches of mathematics?
options: Only financial literacy and measurement
Only statistics and data management
Algebra and geometry
Only basic arithmetic and probability

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Biology: Camouflage, Mimicry, and Predator-Prey Adaptations
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand: camouflage allows organisms to blend into their surroundings to avoid detection, while mimicry involves one species evolving to resemble another, and both are adaptations shaped by natural selection that influence predator-prey relationships in an ecosystem.

quiz.q: What is camouflage?
options: A behaviour found only in plants
A process of digesting food quickly
A method animals use to communicate through sound only
An adaptation that allows organisms to blend into their surroundings

quiz.q: What is mimicry?
options: When a species loses all its distinguishing features
When an animal changes colour randomly with no pattern
When two unrelated species merge into one organism
When one species evolves to resemble another species

quiz.q: Why might a harmless species evolve to mimic a dangerous one?
options: Mimicry has no survival benefit
To deter predators by appearing more threatening than it actually is
To attract more predators intentionally
To become less visible to its own prey only

quiz.q: What evolutionary process shapes adaptations like camouflage and mimicry?
options: A process unrelated to survival
A process that only affects plants
Natural selection
Random, purposeless mutation with no selection pressure

quiz.q: How do camouflage and mimicry influence predator-prey relationships?
options: They shift the balance of detection and evasion between predators and prey
They guarantee predator species always fail to find food
They have no effect on predator-prey interactions
They guarantee prey species always survive

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: The Halibut Treaty of 1923 and Early Canadian Autonomy in Foreign Affairs
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: the Halibut Treaty of 1923 was the first international treaty negotiated and signed by Canada independently of Britain, a landmark step in the development of Canadian sovereignty in foreign affairs that paved the way for later milestones like the Balfour Declaration.

quiz.q: What made the Halibut Treaty of 1923 historically significant?
options: It ended all trade between Canada and the United States
It was the first treaty ever signed by any British colony
It established the Royal Canadian Navy
It was the first international treaty negotiated and signed by Canada independently of Britain

quiz.q: What was the subject of the Halibut Treaty?
options: Immigration quotas
Military alliance terms
Railway construction rights
Fishing rights and conservation in the Pacific

quiz.q: Which country did Canada sign the Halibut Treaty with?
options: The United States
Japan
Russia
France

quiz.q: In what year was the Halibut Treaty signed?
How did the Halibut Treaty pave the way for later developments in Canadian autonomy?
options: It had no connection to later constitutional developments
It ended any further Canadian involvement in foreign affairs
It transferred all foreign policy control back to Britain permanently
It set a precedent for Canada acting independently in foreign affairs, later reinforced by the Balfour Declaration

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: English Review: Grammar, Style, and Contemporary Literacy
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand review: students revisit gerunds and infinitives, stream-of-consciousness narration, the eulogy, postmodern fiction and metafiction, algorithmic bias, pathetic fallacy and personification, the investigative report, appositives, and the trickster figure.

quiz.q: What is a gerund?
options: A verb that shows past tense only
A type of conjunction
A word that replaces a pronoun
A verb form ending in -ing that functions as a noun

quiz.q: What does stream-of-consciousness narration attempt to capture?
options: The continuous, often unstructured flow of a characters thoughts and impressions
Only dialogue spoken between characters
A formal summary of the plot
A strictly chronological sequence of external events

quiz.q: What is metafiction?
options: Storytelling that draws attention to its own fictional nature
A story with no narrator or characters
A purely factual, non-fictional report
A subgenre of poetry only

quiz.q: What is pathetic fallacy?
options: A type of grammatical mistake
Attributing human emotions to nature or weather to reflect a characters mood
A logical error in an argument
A method of citing sources

quiz.q: What defines a trickster figure?
options: A clever, boundary-crossing character who uses wit and deception
A character with no personality traits
A character who always follows every rule strictly
A minor character who never affects the plot

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Math Review: Derivatives, Number Theory, and Advanced Concepts
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand review: students revisit the product and quotient rules, the Euclidean Algorithm, hypothesis testing, partial fraction decomposition, non-Euclidean geometry, mathematical induction, vector projections, Bayes Theorem, and roots of unity.

quiz.q: What does the product rule allow you to differentiate?
options: A function formed by adding two constants
Only trigonometric ratios with no functions involved
A function formed by multiplying two other functions together
Only a single constant term

quiz.q: What does the Euclidean Algorithm calculate?
options: The least common multiple of two fractions only
The greatest common divisor of two integers
The area of a rectangle
The square root of a number

quiz.q: What is a null hypothesis?
options: A hypothesis that is always proven true
A statement with no statistical meaning
A hypothesis with no possible outcome
A default assumption of no effect or no difference

quiz.q: What does the principle of mathematical induction prove?
options: That a statement is true for only one specific number
That a shape has a certain area
That an equation has no solution
That a statement holds true for every natural number

quiz.q: What does Bayes Theorem allow you to do?
options: Find the derivative of a function
Calculate the area of a triangle
Solve a quadratic equation
Update the probability of an event based on new evidence

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Science Review: Human Biology, Chemistry, and Earth Science
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand review: students revisit the integumentary system, buffers and pH regulation, glaciers and ice ages, semiconductors, coral reefs, fossil formation and the geologic time scale, instinct versus learning, the Maillard reaction, and camouflage and mimicry.

quiz.q: What is the skin considered in relation to the human body?
options: A structure unrelated to any body system
An organ found only in mammals with fur
The largest organ of the body
The smallest organ of the body

quiz.q: What is a buffer solution?
options: A solution that resists changes in pH when acid or base is added
A pure solvent with no solute
A solution that always becomes strongly acidic
A solution with no chemical properties

quiz.q: What is a semiconductor?
options: A material that never conducts electricity at all
A material that always conducts electricity perfectly
A material used only for insulation
A material with electrical conductivity between a conductor and an insulator

quiz.q: What do scientists use fossils and rock layers to construct?
options: The geologic time scale
A map of ocean currents
A weather forecasting model
A periodic table of elements

quiz.q: What is camouflage?
options: A behaviour found only in plants
A method animals use to communicate through sound only
A process of digesting food quickly
An adaptation that allows organisms to blend into their surroundings

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: History Review: Canadian Confederation and Constitutional Development
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand review: students revisit the 1919 Paris Peace Conference, the King-Byng Affair, the Manitoba Act, the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Rowell-Sirois Commission, the Manitoba Schools Question, British Columbia and Prince Edward Island joining Confederation, and the Halibut Treaty.

quiz.q: What major agreement was signed at the Paris Peace Conference in 1919?
options: The Treaty of Versailles
The Statute of Westminster
The Balfour Declaration
The Treaty of Ghent

quiz.q: What did Governor General Byng refuse to do in 1926?
options: Call a referendum on Confederation
Dissolve Parliament at Prime Minister Kings request
Sign the Treaty of Versailles
Approve the Balfour Declaration

quiz.q: What did the Manitoba Act of 1870 create?
options: The province of Manitoba
The province of Alberta
The Northwest Territories
The province of Saskatchewan

quiz.q: What promise did the Canadian Pacific Railway fulfill?
options: A promise made during the War of 1812
A promise made to British Columbia upon joining Confederation
A promise made to Quebec after the 1867 Confederation

quiz.q: What made the Halibut Treaty of 1923 historically significant?
options: It ended all trade between Canada and the United States
It established the Royal Canadian Navy
It was the first treaty ever signed by any British colony
It was the first international treaty negotiated and signed by Canada independently of Britain

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Grammar: Correlative Conjunctions
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: correlative conjunctions are paired words such as either/or, neither/nor, both/and, and not only/but also that link balanced words, phrases, or clauses within a sentence.

quiz.q: What is a correlative conjunction?
options: A punctuation mark used in dialogue
A word that replaces a noun entirely
A single word that ends a sentence
A paired word set that links balanced words, phrases, or clauses

quiz.q: Which of the following is a correlative conjunction pair?
options: Run/jump
Book/pen
Quickly/slowly
Either/or

quiz.q: Which sentence correctly uses a correlative conjunction pair?
options: Both the teacher or the students were ready for the test.
Neither the teacher or the students were ready for the test.
Either the teacher and the students were ready for the test.
Neither the teacher nor the students were ready for the test.

quiz.q: Why do correlative conjunctions require parallel structure?
options: They replace the need for a subject entirely
The elements joined should match grammatically for the sentence to read smoothly
They never need to match in form
They only ever join single letters

quiz.q: Which pair means both things are true?
options: Either/or
Neither/nor
Both/and
Whether/or

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Calculus: The Chain Rule for Derivatives
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: the chain rule provides a method for differentiating a composite function, one function nested inside another, by multiplying the derivative of the outer function by the derivative of the inner function.

quiz.q: What does the chain rule allow you to differentiate?
options: A composite function, one function nested inside another
Only whole numbers with no variables
Only a single constant term
Only a sum of two unrelated functions

quiz.q: How is the chain rule generally applied?
options: By ignoring the inner function entirely
By dividing the outer function by the inner function
By adding the two functions together first
By multiplying the derivative of the outer function by the derivative of the inner function

quiz.q: Which type of function most clearly requires the chain rule to differentiate?
options: A function with no inner expression at all
A single constant with no variable
A composite function such as the square of a trigonometric expression
A simple linear function like y equals x

quiz.q: The chain rule builds directly on which earlier differentiation rules?
options: Only basic arithmetic with no calculus involved
Only the quadratic formula
Only the Pythagorean Theorem
The power rule and the basic derivative rules

quiz.q: Why is the chain rule essential in calculus?
options: It eliminates the need for the power rule entirely
Many real functions are composite functions that cannot be differentiated with simpler rules alone
It replaces the need to ever find a derivative
It only applies to functions with no variables

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Biology: Osmosis, Diffusion, and Cell Transport
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand: diffusion is the movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to lower concentration, and osmosis is the specific diffusion of water across a semi-permeable membrane, both essential processes for moving materials into and out of cells.

quiz.q: What is diffusion?
options: A process that occurs only in solids
The movement of particles only against a concentration gradient
The movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to lower concentration
A process requiring the cell to use energy at all times

quiz.q: What is osmosis?
options: The diffusion of water across a semi-permeable membrane
A process that only occurs in the absence of water
The movement of proteins out of a cell
The diffusion of solid particles through a rigid wall

quiz.q: What property of a cell membrane allows osmosis to occur?
options: It has no effect on which substances pass through
It allows every substance through equally
It is completely impermeable to everything
It is semi-permeable, allowing water but not all solutes through

quiz.q: What happens to a cell placed in a highly concentrated salt solution?
options: The cell membrane instantly dissolves
No water movement occurs under any condition
Water tends to enter the cell rapidly with no limit
Water tends to leave the cell, causing it to shrink

quiz.q: Why are diffusion and osmosis important to living cells?
options: They prevent cells from ever exchanging any materials
They stop all cellular processes from occurring
They are only relevant to non-living matter
They allow essential materials like nutrients and water to move into and out of cells

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: The Founding of the North-West Mounted Police in 1873
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: the North-West Mounted Police was established in 1873 by the Canadian government to maintain order, assert Canadian sovereignty, and regulate relations with Indigenous peoples and settlers across the newly acquired western territories.

quiz.q: In what year was the North-West Mounted Police established?
Why did the Canadian government establish the North-West Mounted Police?
options: To defend against an invasion from the United States
To administer the province of Quebec exclusively
To replace the entire federal parliament
To maintain order and assert Canadian sovereignty over the western territories

quiz.q: What present-day Canadian institution evolved from the North-West Mounted Police?
options: The Canadian Armed Forces
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police
The Bank of Canada
The Supreme Court of Canada

quiz.q: The North-West Mounted Police was tasked with regulating relations between settlers and ___.
options: Provincial legislatures in the east
Foreign diplomats in Ottawa
Indigenous peoples across the western territories
International shipping companies

quiz.q: The founding of the North-West Mounted Police is often studied alongside which other western expansion topic?
options: The Halifax Explosion
The settlement of the Canadian Prairies
The Quebec Referendum of 1995

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Reading: Analyzing Extended Metaphor and Conceit
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: an extended metaphor sustains a single comparison across multiple lines or an entire text, and a conceit is an especially elaborate or unconventional extended metaphor that develops a surprising connection between two very different things.

quiz.q: What is an extended metaphor?
options: A metaphor that uses like or as
A single comparison sustained across multiple lines or an entire text
A metaphor that is stated only once and never returned to
A comparison that lasts only a single word

quiz.q: What is a conceit in literary terms?
options: A grammatical error in a poem
A short simile used only once
An especially elaborate or unconventional extended metaphor
A type of rhyme scheme

quiz.q: Why might a poet choose an extended metaphor over a simple comparison?
options: It eliminates the need for imagery entirely
It removes any figurative meaning from the text
It allows the writer to develop a comparison in greater depth and complexity
It forces the writer to abandon the comparison after one line

quiz.q: What makes a conceit feel surprising to a reader?
options: It connects two very different things in an unexpected way
It only compares extremely similar things
It restates the literal meaning directly
It avoids any figurative language

quiz.q: Extended metaphors and conceits are most useful for ___.
options: Replacing dialogue in a narrative
Removing all imagery from a poem
Simplifying a text to a single literal statement
Deepening a texts thematic meaning through a sustained comparison

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Number Theory: Fermats Little Theorem
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: Fermats Little Theorem states that if p is a prime number, then for any integer a not divisible by p, a raised to the power of p minus 1 is congruent to 1 modulo p, a result with important applications in modular arithmetic and cryptography.

quiz.q: What condition must p satisfy in Fermats Little Theorem?
options: p must be equal to zero
p must be an even number only
p must be a prime number
p must be a perfect square

quiz.q: What does Fermats Little Theorem state about a raised to the power p minus 1?
options: It is always equal to zero
It is never a whole number
It is congruent to 1 modulo p, when a is not divisible by p
It always equals exactly p

quiz.q: Fermats Little Theorem builds on which earlier number theory concept?
options: The quadratic formula
Basic long division only
The Pythagorean Theorem
Modular arithmetic

quiz.q: What modern field commonly applies Fermats Little Theorem?
options: Ancient astronomy with no modern use
Elementary counting with no further application
Cryptography and computer security
Basic geometry with no numbers involved

quiz.q: Why is the condition that a is not divisible by p important in the theorem?
options: Without it, the congruence relationship described by the theorem does not hold
It applies only when a equals zero
It only matters when p is not prime
It has no effect on the theorem at all

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Chemistry: Chromatography and Separation Techniques
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand: chromatography is a laboratory technique used to separate the components of a mixture based on how differently each component travels through a stationary medium carried by a moving solvent, revealing the number and identity of substances present.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of chromatography?
options: To separate the components of a mixture
To determine the mass of a solid object
To combine several substances into a single compound
To measure the temperature of a solution

quiz.q: What causes different components to separate during chromatography?
options: Components separate only by changing colour randomly
Each component travels a different distance through the stationary medium at a different rate
All components always travel at exactly the same rate
Separation occurs due to gravity alone with no medium involved

quiz.q: What carries the mixture through the stationary medium in chromatography?
options: A block of ice
A magnetic field
A beam of light only
A moving solvent

quiz.q: What can scientists learn from a completed chromatography experiment?
options: The exact temperature of the room
The number and identity of substances present in a mixture
The electrical charge of the container
The atomic number of every element involved

quiz.q: Chromatography is commonly used in which real-world application?
options: Calculating the area of a triangle
Predicting tomorrows weather
Measuring the speed of a moving vehicle
Forensic analysis of ink or drug samples

subjects.subject: History

subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: the Naval Aid Bill of 1912-13, proposed by Prime Minister Robert Borden to fund British dreadnoughts directly rather than build a Canadian navy, sparked a bitter national debate over Canadas military relationship with Britain and was ultimately defeated in the Senate.

quiz.q: Who proposed the Naval Aid Bill?
options: Prime Minister Mackenzie King

quiz.q: What did the Naval Aid Bill propose to fund?
options: A new Canadian air force
British dreadnoughts directly instead of building a Canadian navy
A national system of highways
The construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway

quiz.q: What ultimately happened to the Naval Aid Bill?
options: It was approved directly by the King
It was never debated at all
It was defeated in the Senate
It passed unanimously in Parliament

quiz.q: What broader issue did the Naval Aid Bill debate reflect?
options: A dispute over provincial boundaries
A disagreement over agricultural tariffs only

quiz.q: The Naval Aid Bill debate occurred in the years immediately before which major conflict?

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Writing: The Public Service Announcement
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: a public service announcement, or PSA, is a brief persuasive message designed to inform or influence public behaviour on an issue of social importance, using a clear call to action, a defined target audience, and a concise, memorable structure.

quiz.q: What is the primary purpose of a public service announcement?
options: To entertain readers with unrelated fiction
To sell a specific commercial product

quiz.q: What is an essential feature of an effective PSA?
options: A complete absence of any purpose
A clear call to action for the audience
An extremely long and detailed narrative
A focus on private, unrelated matters

quiz.q: Why must a PSA writer define a target audience?

Because a PSA should never be shown to anyone

Because PSAs are never meant to be understood

quiz.q: Which of the following is a typical topic for a PSA?

Explaining a mathematical proof
Reviewing a recent novel
Summarizing a historical battle

quiz.q: Why do PSAs typically use concise, memorable language?

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Statistics: Confidence Intervals and Margin of Error
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: a confidence interval is a range of values, calculated from sample data, that is likely to contain the true population parameter, with the margin of error indicating how much the sample estimate might differ from that true value.

quiz.q: What does a confidence interval estimate?
options: The exact value of a population parameter with total certainty
A range of values likely to contain the true population parameter
A single number with no range at all
The size of a sample only

quiz.q: What does the margin of error indicate?
options: How much a sample estimate might differ from the true population value
The colour used in a data visualization
The exact size of the entire population
Whether a hypothesis test was conducted correctly

quiz.q: How does increasing the sample size typically affect the margin of error?
options: It has no effect on the margin of error
It generally decreases the margin of error
It makes the margin of error undefined
It always increases the margin of error

quiz.q: A 95 percent confidence level means ___.
options: Only 5 percent of the data was collected

The sample size must always be exactly 95

quiz.q: Confidence intervals are commonly used alongside which other statistical concept?
options: The Pythagorean Theorem

Basic long division
The quadratic formula

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Physics: Aerodynamics and the Physics of Flight
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand: aerodynamics studies how air interacts with moving objects, and flight depends on four key forces, lift, weight, thrust, and drag, with an aircrafts wing shape generating lift by causing air to move faster over the curved upper surface.

quiz.q: What are the four key forces involved in flight?

Lift, weight, thrust, and drag

Only temperature and pressure

quiz.q: What force allows an aircraft to overcome gravity and rise?

Lift
Weight
Density

It has no effect on the airflow at all

quiz.q: What force acts opposite to thrust during flight?
options: Density
Lift
Weight
Drag

quiz.q: Why do engineers study aerodynamics when designing aircraft?
options: To maximize lift and minimize drag for efficient, stable flight

subjects.subject: History

subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: the Income War Tax Act of 1917 introduced a federal personal income tax in Canada as a temporary wartime measure to help fund Canadas participation in World War I, though the tax was never repealed and became a permanent feature of Canadian federal finances.

quiz.q: What type of tax did the Income War Tax Act introduce federally?
options: A personal income tax
A tax on imported goods only
A property tax on farmland only

quiz.q: The Income War Tax Act is often studied as an example of ___.
options: A tax that was ruled unconstitutional
A policy with no lasting effect on Canada

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Literature: Utopian Fiction and Ideal Societies
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: utopian fiction imagines a society organized around an ideal system of government, technology, or social values, often used by authors to explore what a better world might look like while implicitly critiquing the flaws of contemporary society.

quiz.q: What does utopian fiction typically imagine?
options: A society with no organization of any kind
A purely factual historical account
A world with no characters or setting
