quiz.q: How does utopian fiction differ from dystopian fiction?
options: The two genres are identical with no differences
Utopian fiction always avoids any social commentary
Dystopian fiction always presents a perfect society
Utopian fiction presents an idealized society, while dystopian fiction presents a flawed or oppressive one

quiz.q: Why might an author write utopian fiction?
options: To avoid making any statement about society
To explore what a better world might look like and implicitly critique present society
To eliminate the need for any imaginative elements
To provide a purely factual scientific report

quiz.q: Which of the following might a utopian novel explore?
options: Only a detailed description of weather patterns
An imagined system of governance believed to solve real social problems
Only a list of unrelated statistics
Only a biography of a historical figure

quiz.q: Utopian fiction is often discussed alongside which related genre?
options: Dystopian fiction
Detective fiction
Historical fiction exclusively
Epistolary fiction

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Calculus: Implicit Differentiation
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: implicit differentiation is a technique for finding the derivative of a relation in which y is not isolated as a function of x, by differentiating both sides of an equation with respect to x and applying the chain rule to terms involving y.

quiz.q: When is implicit differentiation typically used?
options: Only when working with whole numbers
Only when an equation has no variables at all
When y is not isolated as a function of x in an equation
Only when a function is already fully simplified for y

quiz.q: What technique is applied to terms involving y during implicit differentiation?
options: Basic long division
The Pythagorean Theorem
The chain rule
The quadratic formula

quiz.q: What is the general first step in implicit differentiation?
options: Differentiating both sides of the equation with respect to x
Solving the equation for y before differentiating anything
Ignoring one side of the equation entirely
Substituting a specific numerical value for x first

quiz.q: Why is implicit differentiation useful for curves like circles?
options: Such curves are not easily written as a single function of x, so implicit methods are needed
Circles require no differentiation at all
Circles never have a defined derivative
Implicit differentiation only works for straight lines

quiz.q: Implicit differentiation is closely related to which other calculus rule?
options: The Euclidean Algorithm
The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic
The chain rule
The Binomial Theorem

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Earth Science: Sinkholes and Karst Topography
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand: karst topography forms when slightly acidic groundwater slowly dissolves soluble bedrock such as limestone, creating underground caves and channels that can collapse suddenly to form sinkholes at the surface.

quiz.q: What type of bedrock is most associated with karst topography?
options: Volcanic ash with no groundwater involved
Metallic ore deposits only
Solid granite with no soluble minerals
Soluble rock such as limestone

quiz.q: What causes karst landscapes to form over time?
options: Rapid freezing of surface water
Slightly acidic groundwater slowly dissolving soluble bedrock
Wind erosion of sand dunes only
Sudden volcanic eruptions

quiz.q: What often forms underground in karst regions before a sinkhole appears?
options: A permanent lake with no connection to the surface
Large deposits of coal
Caves and channels created by dissolved rock
Layers of solid ice

quiz.q: What is a sinkhole?
options: A surface depression formed when underground rock collapses
A type of volcanic mountain
A large body of standing ocean water
A permanent structure built by humans

quiz.q: Why can sinkholes form suddenly and pose a hazard?
options: Sinkholes only occur in areas with no groundwater at all
Underground erosion can weaken rock until it can no longer support the surface above it
Sinkholes have no connection to underground rock structure
Sinkholes always form gradually over centuries with visible warning signs

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: The Formation of Canadian National Railways in 1919
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: Canadian National Railways was formed in 1919 when the federal government consolidated several financially struggling private railway companies into a single publicly owned corporation, creating a major state-run competitor to the privately owned Canadian Pacific Railway.

quiz.q: In what year was Canadian National Railways formed?
Why did the federal government create Canadian National Railways?
options: To replace the Canadian Pacific Railway entirely and shut it down
To transfer all rail service to the United States
To consolidate several financially struggling private railway companies into one public corporation
To build the first railway ever constructed in Canada

quiz.q: What type of ownership did Canadian National Railways represent?
options: Ownership by a foreign government
Ownership by a single individual investor
Entirely private, shareholder-only ownership
Public, government-owned ownership

quiz.q: Canadian National Railways became a major competitor to which existing railway?
options: The Canadian Pacific Railway
The St. Lawrence Seaway
The Trans-Canada Highway
The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway exclusively with no other rivals

quiz.q: What economic condition among private railways led to the creation of Canadian National Railways?
options: Several private railway companies were in serious financial difficulty
All private railways were extremely profitable with no need for support
There were no private railways operating in Canada at the time
Private railways had already been fully nationalized decades earlier

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Media Literacy: Clickbait and the Attention Economy
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: clickbait refers to headlines or content designed primarily to attract clicks rather than to inform accurately, a strategy shaped by the attention economy, in which media companies compete for limited audience attention often at the expense of depth or accuracy.

quiz.q: What is clickbait?
options: A method of fact-checking a news article
A type of formal citation used in academic essays
A grammatical structure used in headlines only
Headlines or content designed primarily to attract clicks rather than inform accurately

quiz.q: What is the attention economy?
options: A method of teaching mathematics
A style of formal academic writing
A system in which media companies compete for limited audience attention
An economic system based only on physical currency

quiz.q: Why might clickbait sacrifice accuracy?
options: Clickbait never uses headlines of any kind
Clickbait always prioritizes factual accuracy above all else
Its main goal is to generate clicks, which can come at the expense of depth or accuracy
Clickbait has no relationship to how content is written

quiz.q: What is one strategy for identifying clickbait headlines?
options: Assuming clickbait never appears on social media
Ignoring the headline and reading only the images
Assuming every headline is completely accurate
Noticing exaggerated or vague language designed to provoke curiosity

quiz.q: Why is understanding the attention economy important for media literacy?
options: It only applies to printed newspapers from the past
It has no relevance to how people consume media
It helps readers recognize how content is designed to capture and hold their attention
It guarantees that all online content is trustworthy

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Geometry: An Introduction to Polar Coordinates
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: the polar coordinate system locates a point using a distance from a fixed origin and an angle from a fixed direction, rather than the horizontal and vertical distances used in the Cartesian system, offering a natural way to describe curves with rotational symmetry.

quiz.q: What two values define a point in the polar coordinate system?
options: Three separate coordinate values
Two perpendicular horizontal and vertical distances only
A distance from the origin and an angle from a fixed direction
A single value with no direction involved

quiz.q: How does the polar coordinate system differ from the Cartesian system?
options: It uses distance and angle instead of horizontal and vertical distances
It uses only negative numbers
It is identical to the Cartesian system in every way
It cannot represent any curves at all

quiz.q: What is the fixed reference point in the polar coordinate system called?
options: The y-intercept
The pole, or origin
The vertex of a triangle
The slope

quiz.q: Polar coordinates are especially useful for describing which type of curve?
options: Only single isolated points with no curve at all
Only straight horizontal lines
Only straight vertical lines
Curves with rotational symmetry, such as spirals or circles

quiz.q: The angle in a polar coordinate is typically measured from ___.
options: The positive horizontal axis
A randomly chosen point with no fixed reference
The center of the y-axis only
The negative vertical axis only

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Biology: Vaccines and Immunization
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand: a vaccine introduces a weakened, inactivated, or partial form of a pathogen into the body, training the immune system to recognize and respond quickly to that pathogen in the future without causing the actual disease.

quiz.q: What does a vaccine typically introduce into the body?
options: A weakened, inactivated, or partial form of a pathogen
A fully active, disease-causing pathogen at full strength
A completely unrelated substance with no biological effect
Only antibiotics with no connection to pathogens

quiz.q: What is the main goal of vaccination?
options: To train the immune system to recognize and respond quickly to a specific pathogen
To immediately cause the full disease in every recipient
To eliminate the need for an immune system entirely
To weaken the immune system permanently

quiz.q: How does the immune system typically respond after vaccination?
options: It produces memory cells that allow a faster response upon future exposure
It attacks only healthy body cells instead
It becomes permanently unable to respond to any pathogen
It forgets the pathogen immediately after exposure

quiz.q: Why do vaccines not typically cause the full disease they protect against?
options: They use a weakened, inactivated, or partial form of the pathogen rather than the full active version
Vaccines only work after a person has already recovered from the disease
Vaccines have no connection to the pathogen at all
They always contain the complete, fully active pathogen

quiz.q: What public health benefit can widespread vaccination provide to a community?
options: No measurable effect on disease spread
A guaranteed elimination of all diseases instantly
Reduced spread of disease through increased population immunity
An immediate increase in disease transmission

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: The Formation of the United Church of Canada in 1925
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: the United Church of Canada was formed in 1925 through the union of the Methodist, Congregationalist, and most Presbyterian churches in Canada, creating the largest Protestant denomination in the country and reflecting a broader movement toward Canadian religious and institutional independence.

quiz.q: In what year was the United Church of Canada formed?
Which churches united to form the United Church of Canada?
options: The Catholic and Anglican churches
The Baptist and Lutheran churches only
A union of every religious denomination in Canada
The Methodist, Congregationalist, and most Presbyterian churches

quiz.q: What did the United Church of Canada become after its formation?
options: A branch of the Catholic Church
The largest Protestant denomination in the country
A small, minor religious group with few members
An officially government-run institution

quiz.q: The formation of the United Church of Canada reflected a broader trend toward ___.
options: The elimination of all religious institutions in Canada
Canadian religious and institutional independence
Continued dependence on British religious authority
A merger with an American religious denomination

quiz.q: Which decade saw the formation of the United Church of Canada?
options: The 1980s
The 1940s
The 1860s
The 1920s

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Grammar: Absolute Phrases
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: an absolute phrase consists of a noun followed by a participle or modifier and describes the surrounding sentence as a whole rather than modifying a single word, adding vivid detail without forming a complete independent clause.

quiz.q: What does an absolute phrase typically consist of?
options: A verb followed directly by a conjunction
A complete independent clause only
A noun followed by a participle or modifier
A single adjective with no noun

quiz.q: What does an absolute phrase usually modify?
options: Nothing at all within the sentence
Only a preposition
Only a single pronoun
The entire sentence rather than a single word

quiz.q: Which sentence contains an absolute phrase?
options: The letter, which arrived yesterday, was opened.
She opened the letter because she was curious.
Her hands trembling, she opened the letter slowly.
She opened the letter slowly.

quiz.q: Why might a writer use an absolute phrase?
options: To add vivid, specific detail without forming a full independent clause
To make the sentence grammatically incomplete on purpose
To replace the main verb of the sentence entirely
To avoid using any nouns in a sentence

quiz.q: How is an absolute phrase typically set off in a sentence?
options: With a colon introducing a formal list
With a semicolon connecting two full clauses
With no punctuation of any kind
With a comma separating it from the rest of the sentence

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Discrete Math: The Pigeonhole Principle
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: the pigeonhole principle states that if more items are placed into containers than there are containers, at least one container must hold more than one item, a simple idea with surprisingly powerful applications in proofs and problem solving.

quiz.q: What does the pigeonhole principle state?
options: No container can ever hold more than one item
The number of items must always equal the number of containers
If more items are placed into containers than there are containers, at least one container holds more than one item
Every container must hold exactly one item at all times

quiz.q: What is required for the pigeonhole principle to guarantee a container with multiple items?
options: The number of items must exceed the number of containers
The number of items must be exactly equal to the number of containers
The number of containers must exceed the number of items
There must be zero items in total

quiz.q: The pigeonhole principle is especially useful for ___.
options: Proving that a certain outcome must occur without needing to check every case
Calculating a derivative directly
Finding the exact probability of a single event
Measuring the exact area of a shape

quiz.q: Which scenario illustrates the pigeonhole principle?
options: If zero people are in a room, two must share a birth month
If 13 people are in a room, at least two must share a birth month
The principle only applies to numbers larger than one million
If 12 people are in a room, each must have a different birth month

quiz.q: Why is the pigeonhole principle considered powerful despite its simplicity?
options: It requires checking every single case individually with no shortcuts
It only applies to geometry problems
It has no real mathematical applications
It can prove certain results must be true without exhaustively checking every possibility

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Chemistry: Water Purification and Treatment
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand: water purification uses physical and chemical processes such as filtration, coagulation, and disinfection to remove contaminants, pathogens, and particulates from water, making it safe for human consumption and other uses.

quiz.q: What is the main goal of water purification?
options: To eliminate water entirely from a supply system
To convert all water into a solid state
To add as many impurities to water as possible
To remove contaminants, pathogens, and particulates from water

quiz.q: What process uses a physical barrier to remove larger particles from water?
options: Sublimation
Titration
Combustion
Filtration

quiz.q: What is coagulation used for in water treatment?
options: Clumping together small particles so they can be more easily removed
Increasing the temperature of the water rapidly
Removing all oxygen from the water supply
Adding colour to clear water

quiz.q: What is the purpose of disinfection in water treatment?
options: To remove all minerals from the water permanently
To kill or inactivate harmful pathogens in the water
To make the water less safe to drink
To add more bacteria to the water supply

quiz.q: Why is safe drinking water treatment important for public health?
options: It has no effect on human health at all
It is only relevant in areas with no population
It helps prevent the spread of waterborne diseases
It always increases the risk of illness

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: The Old Age Pensions Act of 1927
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: the Old Age Pensions Act of 1927 established Canadas first federal old age pension program, providing modest, means-tested financial support to low-income seniors and marking an early step toward the modern Canadian social welfare system.

quiz.q: In what year was the Old Age Pensions Act passed?
What did the Old Age Pensions Act establish?
options: A national healthcare system for all Canadians
A national unemployment insurance program
Canadas first federal old age pension program
A federal minimum wage law

quiz.q: Who was eligible to receive support under the original Old Age Pensions Act?
options: Only federal government employees
Only wealthy retired business owners
All Canadians regardless of age or income
Low-income seniors, based on a means test

quiz.q: The Old Age Pensions Act is considered an early step toward what broader system?
options: The modern Canadian social welfare system
The Canadian tax appeals system
The provincial court system
The Canadian military justice system

quiz.q: What term describes a program that provides benefits based on an applicants income level?
options: Privately insured only
Universally funded with no conditions
Available only to corporations
Means-tested

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Reading: Analyzing Narrative Distance and Psychic Distance
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: narrative distance, sometimes called psychic distance, describes how close or removed a narrator feels from a characters inner thoughts and emotions, ranging from an intimate, close perspective to a detached, observational one.

quiz.q: What does narrative distance describe?
options: How close or removed a narrator feels from a characters inner thoughts and emotions
The number of pages in a chapter
The physical distance between two settings in a story
The time period in which a story is set

quiz.q: What is another common term for narrative distance?
options: Plot structure
Psychic distance
Dramatic irony
Rising action

quiz.q: What characterizes a close narrative distance?
options: A perspective with no connection to any character at all
A viewpoint that only reports distant historical facts
An intimate perspective that closely follows a characters inner thoughts and feelings
A narrator who never describes any emotion

quiz.q: What characterizes a far or detached narrative distance?
options: An extremely close, intimate view of a single characters emotions
A more observational, removed perspective on events and characters
A total absence of any narration
A perspective that only exists in dialogue

quiz.q: Why might an author shift narrative distance within a text?
options: To eliminate the need for a plot
To control how intimately readers connect with a character at different moments
To confuse readers with no clear purpose
To remove the narrator from the story entirely

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Calculus: Related Rates
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: related rates problems use implicit differentiation to determine how the rate of change of one quantity relates to the rate of change of another quantity, when both are connected by an equation and changing with respect to time.

quiz.q: What do related rates problems determine?
options: The exact value of a single unrelated quantity
The colour of an object in a diagram
Only the area of a fixed, unchanging shape
How the rate of change of one quantity relates to the rate of change of another

quiz.q: What technique is central to solving related rates problems?
options: Implicit differentiation with respect to time
Measuring an object directly with a ruler only
Basic addition of two constants
Simple counting with no equations involved

quiz.q: In a related rates problem, quantities are typically connected by ___.
options: A relationship involving only whole numbers
No mathematical relationship at all
An equation relating the two changing quantities
A relationship that never changes over time

quiz.q: Why is time often the variable with respect to which related rates are differentiated?
options: Because time is always held constant in these problems
Because the quantities involved are described as changing over time
Because related rates problems never involve change
Because time never appears in these problems

quiz.q: A classic example of a related rates problem involves ___.
options: Finding how fast the radius of a balloon increases as it is inflated
Measuring the weight of a balloon at rest
Finding the exact colour of a balloon
Counting the total number of balloons in a room

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: The Excretory System: Kidneys and Waste Removal
subjects.summary: Grade 8 Science strand: the excretory system, especially the kidneys, filters waste products and excess water from the blood, producing urine and helping maintain the bodys internal balance.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: The Excretory System: Kidneys and Waste Removal

quiz.q: What is the main function of the excretory system?
options: Digesting food in the stomach
Producing sound for speech
Filtering waste products and excess water from the blood
Pumping blood throughout the body

quiz.q: Which organs are the primary filters in the excretory system?
options: The heart
The lungs
The liver only
The kidneys

quiz.q: What waste product do the kidneys help remove from the body?
options: Only sweat
Urine, containing filtered waste and excess water
Only saliva
Only carbon dioxide

quiz.q: Why is maintaining fluid balance in the body important?
options: It supports proper function of cells and organs
Only muscles are affected by fluid balance
The body never needs to balance fluids
Fluid balance has no effect on the body

quiz.q: The excretory system works to keep the bodys internal environment ___.
options: Completely dependent on outside temperature

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: The Canadian Radio Broadcasting Act and the Founding of the CBC
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Act of 1932 created a national public broadcaster to counter growing American radio influence and unify the country through shared programming, a role later expanded when the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was formally established in 1936.

quiz.q: What did the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Act of 1932 create?
options: A national public broadcaster
A new national police force
A national railway system
A federal income tax

quiz.q: Why did the federal government establish a national public broadcaster?
options: To eliminate all radio broadcasting in Canada permanently
To counter growing American radio influence and unify the country through shared programming
To fund the construction of a national railway
To transfer all broadcasting control to private American companies

quiz.q: In what year was the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation formally established?
What common national concern motivated the creation of a public broadcaster in the 1930s?
options: Concern that American radio signals were dominating Canadian audiences
A dispute over provincial voting rights
A lack of any interest in radio technology
A shortage of newspapers across the country

quiz.q: The founding of the CBC reflects a broader theme of which era in Canadian history?
options: Efforts to strengthen Canadian cultural identity and institutions
The complete rejection of all modern technology

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Writing: The Abstract and Executive Summary
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: an abstract or executive summary is a concise overview placed at the start of a longer document that summarizes its purpose, key findings, and conclusions, allowing readers to quickly understand the content without reading the entire text.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of an abstract or executive summary?
options: To replace the entire document with no other content needed
To introduce unrelated information not found in the document
To provide a detailed, page-by-page retelling of the document
To provide a concise overview of a longer documents purpose, findings, and conclusions

quiz.q: Where is an abstract or executive summary typically placed in a document?
options: At the start of the document
Only in a separate, unrelated document
Only in a footnote at the very end
Scattered randomly throughout the middle of the text

quiz.q: Why do readers value a well-written abstract or executive summary?
options: It intentionally omits the main purpose of the document
It forces them to read the full document twice
It allows them to quickly understand the content without reading the entire text
It removes the need for the document to have any conclusion

quiz.q: Which of the following should typically be included in an abstract?
options: Only unrelated personal opinions
The key findings and conclusions of the document
Advertisements unrelated to the documents topic
A list of every sentence in the original document

quiz.q: Why should an abstract or executive summary be concise?
options: So readers can grasp the essential content efficiently before deciding to read further
Because conciseness prevents any information from being understood
Because it must always be longer than the original document
Because concise writing has no value in professional communication

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Number Theory: Diophantine Equations
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: a Diophantine equation is a polynomial equation for which only integer solutions are sought, a concept named after the ancient mathematician Diophantus that connects algebra and number theory in problems ranging from simple linear equations to complex modern applications.

quiz.q: What distinguishes a Diophantine equation from a typical algebraic equation?
options: A Diophantine equation only allows decimal solutions
A Diophantine equation can never be solved
A Diophantine equation has no variables at all
Only integer solutions are sought for a Diophantine equation

quiz.q: Who is the Diophantine equation named after?
options: The mathematician Euclid
The mathematician Pythagoras
The mathematician Fermat
The ancient mathematician Diophantus

quiz.q: What branches of mathematics does the study of Diophantine equations connect?
options: Algebra and number theory
Only basic geometry with no algebra involved
Only trigonometry with no number theory involved
Only statistics with no algebra involved

quiz.q: Which of the following is an example of a simple linear Diophantine equation?
options: 3x + 5y = 7, solved for integer x and y
An equation with no possible integer solutions defined by its structure
An equation requiring only decimal answers
A single equation with no variables

quiz.q: Why are Diophantine equations still studied in modern mathematics?
options: They connect to important applications, including areas of modern cryptography
They have no remaining relevance to any field
They were fully solved by ancient mathematicians with nothing left to study
They apply only to ancient historical problems with no modern use

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Earth Science: Wetlands and Their Ecological Role
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand: wetlands are transitional ecosystems where land is saturated with water for significant periods, supporting high biodiversity while providing critical services such as filtering pollutants, controlling floods, and storing carbon.

quiz.q: What defines a wetland ecosystem?
options: Land that is always completely dry with no water present
An area made entirely of solid rock with no vegetation
A region located only at the top of a mountain
Land that is saturated with water for significant periods of time

quiz.q: Why are wetlands known for high biodiversity?
options: They support no living organisms at all
They are entirely devoid of water and nutrients
They provide a unique habitat that supports a wide range of plant and animal species
They contain only a single species of plant

quiz.q: What water-related service do wetlands provide to surrounding areas?
options: Filtering pollutants and helping control floods
Adding pollutants directly into groundwater
Increasing the risk of flooding in every case
Removing all water from a region permanently

quiz.q: How do wetlands contribute to addressing climate change?
options: They store significant amounts of carbon
They release stored carbon with no absorption at all
They only affect local temperature and nothing else
They have no relationship to carbon storage

quiz.q: Why might human development pose a threat to wetlands?
options: Wetlands are unaffected by any human activity
Wetlands cannot be altered by construction of any kind
Draining or building over wetlands can destroy their unique ecological functions
Human development always improves wetland health

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: Newfoundland and the Commission of Government of 1934
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: facing financial collapse during the Great Depression, the Dominion of Newfoundland suspended its own self-government in 1934 and was administered by an appointed Commission of Government under British oversight until Newfoundland eventually joined Canada in 1949.

quiz.q: Why did Newfoundland suspend its self-government in 1934?
options: It had discovered a large new source of wealth
It had just won a major war
It had just joined Confederation
It faced financial collapse during the Great Depression

quiz.q: What replaced Newfoundlands elected government in 1934?
options: A newly elected democratic parliament
An appointed Commission of Government under British oversight
A government run entirely by the United States
An immediate merger with the province of Quebec

quiz.q: What was Newfoundlands political status before 1934?
options: A Canadian province
A self-governing Dominion
An independent republic with no ties to Britain
A colony of France

quiz.q: What eventually happened to Newfoundland after this period of commission government?
options: It remained under commission government indefinitely with no change
It became fully independent with no ties to any nation
It joined Canada as a province in 1949
It was annexed permanently by the United States

quiz.q: The Commission of Government period illustrates the impact of which global economic event?
options: The Great Depression
World War I
The Klondike Gold Rush
The 1918-1920 Spanish Flu Pandemic

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Literature: The Doppelganger Motif in Fiction
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: a doppelganger is a characters double or look-alike, often representing a hidden or opposing side of the original characters personality, and the motif is frequently used to explore themes of identity, morality, and psychological duality.

quiz.q: What is a doppelganger in literature?
options: A setting that changes throughout a story
A minor character who never returns after one scene
A characters double or look-alike
A narrator who addresses the reader directly

quiz.q: What does a doppelganger often represent in a text?
options: A change in the storys physical setting
A completely unrelated character with no connection to the protagonist
A hidden or opposing side of the original characters personality
A summary of the entire plot

quiz.q: Which theme is the doppelganger motif frequently used to explore?
options: The chronology of historical events
The geography of a fictional country
The economics of a fictional marketplace
Identity and psychological duality

quiz.q: Why might an author use a doppelganger to develop a character?
options: To eliminate the need for any conflict in the story
To simplify the plot into a single, unbroken line
To avoid developing the main character at all
To externalize inner conflict or hidden aspects of the characters identity

quiz.q: The doppelganger motif often creates a sense of ___.
options: Unease or psychological tension between the double and the original character
A purely comedic and lighthearted tone in every case
A total absence of thematic meaning
Complete comfort with no tension whatsoever

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Probability: The Poisson Distribution
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: the Poisson distribution models the probability of a given number of events occurring in a fixed interval of time or space, when those events happen independently and at a known constant average rate.

quiz.q: What does the Poisson distribution model?
options: The exact height of a geometric shape
The probability of an event that never occurs
The probability of a given number of events occurring in a fixed interval of time or space
The area under a straight line only

quiz.q: What condition must the events satisfy for a Poisson distribution to apply?
options: The events must be entirely dependent on one another
The events must occur independently and at a known constant average rate
The events must occur with no defined average rate at all
The events must always occur at the exact same instant

quiz.q: Which of the following is a typical real-world example modeled by a Poisson distribution?
options: The number of customer arrivals at a store in one hour
The colour of a randomly selected object
The temperature of a room at a single moment
The exact height of a single building

quiz.q: How does the Poisson distribution differ from the binomial distribution?
options: The binomial distribution cannot be used to model any real event
The Poisson distribution models counts of events over a continuous interval rather than a fixed number of trials
The Poisson distribution only applies to exactly two possible outcomes
The two distributions are mathematically identical in every way

quiz.q: Why is the average rate parameter important in a Poisson distribution?
options: It has no effect on the resulting probabilities
It only matters when the average rate equals zero
It replaces the need for any probability calculation
It determines the expected number of events in the given interval

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Biology: Bioluminescence in Living Organisms
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand: bioluminescence is the production of light by a living organism through a chemical reaction, most commonly involving the molecule luciferin and the enzyme luciferase, and is used by many marine and terrestrial species for communication, predation, or defense.

quiz.q: What is bioluminescence?
options: A permanent change in an organisms skeletal structure
The absorption of light by a completely inanimate object
The production of light by a living organism through a chemical reaction
A process found only in plants with no animals involved

quiz.q: Which molecule is most commonly involved in producing bioluminescent light?
options: Hemoglobin
Luciferin
Glucose
Chlorophyll

quiz.q: What role does the enzyme luciferase play in bioluminescence?
options: It has no connection to light production at all
It converts light directly into heat with no reaction involved
It catalyzes the chemical reaction that produces light
It prevents any chemical reaction from occurring

quiz.q: Which environment is well known for a high number of bioluminescent species?
options: The surface of the moon
The deep ocean
A completely dry desert with no other adaptations
The inside of a volcano

quiz.q: What is one reason organisms use bioluminescence?
options: To attract prey, communicate, or deter predators
To permanently blind themselves with no other purpose
To increase their body temperature significantly
To eliminate their need for any other senses

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: The Founding of the Bank of Canada in 1934-1935
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: the Bank of Canada was established through legislation passed in 1934 and began operations in 1935 as the countrys central bank, tasked with managing monetary policy, issuing currency, and stabilizing the economy in the aftermath of the Great Depression.

quiz.q: When did the Bank of Canada begin operations?
What role does the Bank of Canada serve?
options: It functions as a provincial tax collection agency
It functions as a private commercial bank only
It functions as a national railway company
It functions as the countrys central bank

quiz.q: What economic crisis contributed to the founding of the Bank of Canada?
options: World War I
The 1918-1920 Spanish Flu Pandemic
The Great Depression
The Klondike Gold Rush

quiz.q: Which of the following is a key responsibility of the Bank of Canada?
options: Building and maintaining national highways
Operating public schools across the country
Managing monetary policy and issuing currency
Administering provincial elections

quiz.q: Why might a country establish a central bank during a major economic crisis?
options: To help stabilize the economy through coordinated monetary policy
To transfer all economic control to a foreign government
To ensure that no economic policy is ever coordinated nationally
To eliminate the need for any currency at all

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: English Review: Grammar, Rhetoric, and Contemporary Literacy
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand review: students revisit correlative conjunctions, extended metaphor and conceit, the public service announcement, utopian fiction, clickbait and the attention economy, absolute phrases, narrative distance, the abstract and executive summary, and the doppelganger motif.

quiz.q: What is a correlative conjunction?
options: A word that replaces a noun entirely
A single word that ends a sentence
A paired word set that links balanced words, phrases, or clauses
A punctuation mark used in dialogue

quiz.q: What is a conceit in literary terms?
options: A type of rhyme scheme
A grammatical error in a poem
A short simile used only once
An especially elaborate or unconventional extended metaphor

quiz.q: What is clickbait?
options: A method of fact-checking a news article
Headlines or content designed primarily to attract clicks rather than inform accurately
A grammatical structure used in headlines only
A type of formal citation used in academic essays

quiz.q: What does an absolute phrase typically consist of?
options: A single adjective with no noun
A noun followed by a participle or modifier
A complete independent clause only
A verb followed directly by a conjunction

quiz.q: What is a doppelganger in literature?
options: A setting that changes throughout a story
A narrator who addresses the reader directly
A characters double or look-alike
A minor character who never returns after one scene

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Math Review: Calculus, Number Theory, and Advanced Concepts
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand review: students revisit the chain rule, Fermats Little Theorem, confidence intervals, implicit differentiation, polar coordinates, the pigeonhole principle, related rates, Diophantine equations, and the Poisson distribution.

quiz.q: What does the chain rule allow you to differentiate?
options: Only whole numbers with no variables
Only a single constant term
A composite function, one function nested inside another
Only a sum of two unrelated functions

quiz.q: What condition must p satisfy in Fermats Little Theorem?
options: p must be an even number only
p must be a perfect square
p must be equal to zero
p must be a prime number

quiz.q: What does a confidence interval estimate?
options: A single number with no range at all
The size of a sample only
A range of values likely to contain the true population parameter
The exact value of a population parameter with total certainty

quiz.q: What does the pigeonhole principle state?
options: Every container must hold exactly one item at all times
No container can ever hold more than one item
If more items are placed into containers than there are containers, at least one container holds more than one item
The number of items must always equal the number of containers

quiz.q: What does the Poisson distribution model?
options: The area under a straight line only
The probability of a given number of events occurring in a fixed interval of time or space
The exact height of a geometric shape
The probability of an event that never occurs

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Science Review: Cell Processes, Chemistry, and Earth Systems
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand review: students revisit osmosis and diffusion, chromatography, aerodynamics and the physics of flight, sinkholes and karst topography, vaccines and immunization, water purification, superconductivity, wetlands, and bioluminescence.

quiz.q: What is diffusion?
options: A process that occurs only in solids
The movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to lower concentration
A process requiring the cell to use energy at all times
The movement of particles only against a concentration gradient

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of chromatography?
options: To combine several substances into a single compound
To separate the components of a mixture
To measure the temperature of a solution
To determine the mass of a solid object

quiz.q: What are the four key forces involved in flight?
options: Only speed and mass
Lift, weight, thrust, and drag
Only gravity and friction
Only temperature and pressure

quiz.q: What defines a superconducting material?
options: It only conducts electricity at extremely high temperatures
It never conducts electricity under any condition
It always resists electrical current completely at every temperature
It conducts electricity with zero electrical resistance below a critical temperature

quiz.q: What is bioluminescence?
options: The absorption of light by a completely inanimate object
The production of light by a living organism through a chemical reaction
A process found only in plants with no animals involved
A permanent change in an organisms skeletal structure

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: History Review: Institution-Building in Early Twentieth-Century Canada
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand review: students revisit the founding of the North-West Mounted Police, the Naval Aid Bill, the Income War Tax Act of 1917, the formation of Canadian National Railways, the founding of the United Church of Canada, the Old Age Pensions Act, the founding of the CBC, Newfoundlands Commission of Government, and the founding of the Bank of Canada.

quiz.q: In what year was the North-West Mounted Police established?
What did the Naval Aid Bill propose to fund?
options: A national system of highways
A new Canadian air force
British dreadnoughts directly instead of building a Canadian navy
The construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway

quiz.q: What was the original stated purpose of the Income War Tax Act?
options: A tax designed to fund the Canadian Pacific Railway
A permanent replacement for all provincial taxes
A temporary wartime measure to help fund Canadas participation in World War I
A tax created to fund Confederation celebrations

quiz.q: What did the Old Age Pensions Act establish?
options: Canadas first federal old age pension program
A federal minimum wage law
A national healthcare system for all Canadians
A national unemployment insurance program

quiz.q: What role does the Bank of Canada serve?
options: It functions as a national railway company
It functions as the countrys central bank
It functions as a provincial tax collection agency
It functions as a private commercial bank only

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Media Literacy: Analyzing Product Placement in Film and Television
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: product placement is the practice of featuring a branded product or service within a film, television show, or other media content in exchange for payment or promotional consideration, blurring the line between entertainment and advertising.

quiz.q: What is product placement?
options: A branded product or service featured within media content in exchange for payment or promotion
A type of movie theatre seating arrangement
A legal requirement for all television broadcasts
A method of editing film footage after production

quiz.q: What line does product placement blur?
options: The line between fiction and historical fact
The line between comedy and tragedy
The line between print and digital media
The line between entertainment and advertising

quiz.q: Why might a viewer fail to notice product placement?
options: Because television programs are required to pause before showing a brand
Because product placement is always announced loudly before it appears
Because it is woven into the story or setting rather than presented as a separate advertisement
Because product placement never appears in visual media

quiz.q: Which of the following is an example of product placement?
options: A newspaper article reviewing a new product
A billboard advertisement seen while driving to a theatre
A character in a film prominently using a specific named brand of laptop
A standalone thirty-second commercial break between scenes

quiz.q: Why is media literacy useful for recognizing product placement?
options: It has no connection to how audiences interpret visual media
It helps viewers distinguish between organic story content and paid promotional material
It guarantees that all media content is free of any advertising
It removes the need to ever watch a film critically

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Calculus: Optimization Problems Using Derivatives
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: optimization problems use derivatives to find the maximum or minimum value of a quantity, typically by setting the derivative of a function equal to zero to locate critical points and then testing which point yields the greatest or least value.

quiz.q: What do optimization problems in calculus typically find?
options: The maximum or minimum value of a quantity
The total number of variables in an equation
The exact colour of a graphed function
The name of the mathematician who first studied the function

quiz.q: What is the first step commonly used to locate a critical point?
options: Multiplying the function by a random constant
Graphing the function without calculating anything
Setting the derivative of the function equal to zero
Ignoring the function entirely and guessing an answer

quiz.q: What is a critical point in an optimization problem?
options: A point defined only by its y-intercept
A point that never appears on a graph
A point where the function is always negative
A point where the derivative is zero or undefined

quiz.q: Why must a critical point be tested after it is found?
options: To determine whether it represents a maximum, a minimum, or neither
Because testing a critical point is never necessary
Because critical points are always automatically the maximum
To convert the critical point into a whole number

quiz.q: Which real-world scenario is a classic example of an optimization problem?
options: Counting the total number of boxes in a warehouse
Finding the dimensions that minimize the material used to build a box of fixed volume
Determining the manufacturer of a randomly selected box
Measuring the exact colour of a box

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Biology: Coevolution and Mutualistic Relationships
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand: coevolution occurs when two or more species reciprocally influence each others evolution over time, often producing mutualistic relationships in which both species benefit, such as flowering plants and their pollinators.

quiz.q: What is coevolution?
options: A process that only occurs in extinct species
A process in which a single species evolves with no influence from any other organism
A sudden, one-time genetic mutation with no evolutionary effect
A process in which two or more species reciprocally influence each others evolution over time

quiz.q: What is a mutualistic relationship?
options: A relationship in which one species is harmed and the other is unaffected
A relationship in which both species are harmed equally
A relationship in which both interacting species benefit
A relationship that only occurs between members of the same species

quiz.q: Which pairing is a classic example of coevolved mutualism?
options: Flowering plants and their pollinators
A shark and a school of unrelated fish with no interaction
Two unrelated species that never interact
A rock and the moss growing nearby with no exchange of benefit

quiz.q: Why might a flower and its pollinator evolve matching physical traits?
options: Because traits that improve the exchange of nectar for pollination benefit both species over generations
Because pollinators always harm the flowers they visit
Because matching traits occur randomly with no evolutionary benefit
Because flowers and pollinators never influence one anothers traits

quiz.q: How does coevolution differ from a relationship where only one species benefits?
options: Coevolution never involves more than one species
In coevolved mutualism both species gain an advantage, while in relationships like parasitism only one species benefits
There is no meaningful difference between mutualism and parasitism
Coevolution always harms both species involved

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: The On-to-Ottawa Trek of 1935
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: the On-to-Ottawa Trek was a 1935 protest march in which unemployed men from federal relief camps travelled by rail from British Columbia toward Ottawa to demand better wages and conditions, ending when the trek was stopped by police in Regina, resulting in the Regina Riot.

quiz.q: What was the On-to-Ottawa Trek?
options: A 1935 protest march by unemployed men from federal relief camps travelling toward Ottawa
A railway construction project connecting British Columbia to Ontario
A diplomatic mission sent to negotiate with the United States
A ceremonial parade celebrating Canadian Confederation

quiz.q: What were the trekkers protesting?
options: A proposed reduction in provincial voting rights
Poor wages and conditions in federal relief camps
A new federal tax on farm equipment
The construction of a new national railway

quiz.q: How did the trekkers initially travel toward Ottawa?
options: By flying in chartered aircraft
By sailing along the Pacific coast
By walking the entire distance on foot with no vehicles
By riding freight trains

quiz.q: Where was the trek ultimately stopped?
options: In Ottawa, Ontario, after arriving successfully
In Regina, Saskatchewan
In Halifax, Nova Scotia
In Vancouver, British Columbia, before it began

quiz.q: What violent event resulted when the trek was stopped?
options: The Halifax Explosion
The Regina Riot
The Oka Crisis
The Winnipeg General Strike

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Grammar: Cleft Sentences for Emphasis
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: a cleft sentence divides a single idea into two clauses, typically using a phrase such as It was... that or What... is to shift emphasis onto a particular piece of information within a sentence.

quiz.q: What does a cleft sentence do?
options: It removes all punctuation from a sentence
It converts a sentence into a question automatically
It divides a single idea into two clauses to shift emphasis onto a particular piece of information
It combines two unrelated ideas into a single run-on sentence

quiz.q: Which sentence opener commonly signals a cleft sentence?
options: It was... that
On the other hand
In conclusion
Once upon a time

quiz.q: Which sentence is an example of a cleft sentence?
options: The coach called the final play.
Calling the final play, the coach smiled.
It was the coach who called the final play.
The coach, who arrived late, called the final play.

quiz.q: Why might a writer choose a cleft sentence over a plain statement?
options: To draw the readers attention to a specific detail within the sentence
To make the sentence impossible to understand
To avoid using a subject or verb entirely
To remove all meaning from the sentence

quiz.q: What type of clause commonly follows the emphasized element in a cleft sentence?
options: A question with no connection to the emphasized element
A completely unrelated independent sentence
A single isolated noun with no clause at all
A relative clause beginning with that or who

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Number Theory: Wilsons Theorem
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: Wilsons Theorem states that a whole number p greater than 1 is prime if and only if (p minus 1) factorial plus 1 is divisible by p, offering a distinctive test for primality rooted in factorials and modular arithmetic.

quiz.q: What does Wilsons Theorem provide a test for?
options: Whether a shape is a regular polygon
Whether a number is even
Whether a fraction is in lowest terms
Whether a number is prime

quiz.q: What quantity does Wilsons Theorem involve, in addition to the number p?
options: The factorial of p minus 1
The square root of p
The logarithm of p
The sine of p degrees

quiz.q: According to Wilsons Theorem, if p is prime, what must be true about (p minus 1) factorial plus 1?
options: It is always a negative number
It is always equal to zero
It is divisible by p
It is never a whole number

quiz.q: What area of mathematics connects most directly to Wilsons Theorem?
options: Modular arithmetic and number theory
Trigonometric identities
Coordinate geometry
Statistical sampling methods

quiz.q: Why is Wilsons Theorem considered mostly a theoretical rather than practical primality test?
options: Factorials are never used in mathematics
It only works for the number zero
Calculating a large factorial becomes computationally expensive very quickly
Prime numbers do not exist above one hundred

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Antibiotic Resistance: A Modern Challenge
subjects.summary: Grade 8 Science strand: antibiotic resistance occurs when bacteria evolve to survive medicines designed to kill them, a growing global health challenge driven partly by the overuse and misuse of antibiotics.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Antibiotic Resistance: A Modern Challenge

quiz.q: What is antibiotic resistance?
options: When bacteria evolve to survive medicines designed to kill them
When a virus becomes weaker over time
When bacteria disappear completely
When a medicine works better over time

quiz.q: What is one major cause of increasing antibiotic resistance?
options: Using antibiotics too rarely
The overuse and misuse of antibiotics
Eating a balanced diet
Regular exercise

quiz.q: Why is antibiotic resistance considered a global health challenge?
options: It has no effect on human health
It makes some bacterial infections much harder to treat
It only affects animals, never humans
It makes all infections easier to cure

quiz.q: What can individuals do to help reduce antibiotic resistance?
options: Share leftover antibiotics with others
Take antibiotics for every illness, including viral infections
Only take antibiotics when prescribed and finish the full course
Stop taking antibiotics as soon as symptoms improve

quiz.q: Antibiotic resistance is an example of what broader biological process?
options: Natural selection acting on bacterial populations
A process unrelated to evolution
A process that only affects humans
A permanently fixed, unchanging trait

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: The Padlock Law of Quebec, 1937
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: the Padlock Law, passed by the Quebec government in 1937, allowed authorities to shut and padlock any premises used to propagate communism or bolshevism without a trial, a measure later challenged as an infringement on civil liberties.

quiz.q: In what year was the Padlock Law passed?
Which government passed the Padlock Law?
options: The government of Quebec
The government of British Columbia
The government of Ontario
The federal government of Canada

quiz.q: What could authorities do under the Padlock Law?
options: Grant additional voting rights to every citizen
Shut and padlock any premises used to propagate communism or bolshevism without a trial
Fund new provincial highways across Quebec
Establish a new provincial bank

quiz.q: What broader concern did the Padlock Law later raise?
options: Concerns about international trade tariffs
Concerns about civil liberties and freedom of expression
Concerns about railway safety standards
Concerns about the price of wheat

quiz.q: What legal concept did critics argue the Padlock Law violated by allowing action without a trial?
options: Responsible government
Free trade
Due process
Universal suffrage

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Reading: Analyzing Allusion in Literature
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: an allusion is a brief, indirect reference to a person, place, event, or work from history, mythology, religion, or another text, allowing a writer to add layered meaning by connecting a new work to a shared body of prior knowledge.

quiz.q: What is an allusion?
options: A detailed, fully explained retelling of another entire story
A grammatical error found within a sentence
A punctuation mark used to end a question
A brief, indirect reference to a person, place, event, or work outside the text

quiz.q: What kinds of sources might an allusion draw from?
options: Only weather reports
History, mythology, religion, or another literary work
Only mathematical formulas
Only grammar textbooks

quiz.q: Why might a writer use allusion?
options: To add layered meaning by connecting the text to a shared body of prior knowledge
To avoid using any figurative language whatsoever
To ensure that no reader can understand the text at all
To remove any connection between the text and outside knowledge

quiz.q: What is required of a reader to fully understand an allusion?
options: A complete misunderstanding of the text
No prior knowledge of any kind
Familiarity with the outside reference being made
Fluency in a foreign language unrelated to the reference

quiz.q: Which of the following is an example of an allusion?
options: Stating the exact time of day in a scene
Describing a room as painted blue
Describing a difficult task as a Herculean effort
Listing the ingredients of a recipe

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Statistics: The Chi-Squared Goodness-of-Fit Test
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: the chi-squared goodness-of-fit test compares observed categorical data to the frequencies that would be expected under a specific hypothesis, producing a statistic that indicates whether the observed data significantly differs from what was expected.

quiz.q: What does a chi-squared goodness-of-fit test compare?
options: Observed categorical data to the frequencies expected under a specific hypothesis
The volume of two different solids
The slope of two unrelated lines
The derivative of a function at a single point

quiz.q: What type of data is the chi-squared goodness-of-fit test designed to analyze?
options: Only irrational numbers
Categorical data
Only data with exactly two data points
Only data with negative values

quiz.q: What does a large chi-squared statistic generally suggest?
options: No hypothesis was ever tested
The observed data significantly differs from what was expected
The sample size was too large to be valid
The observed data matches the expected data perfectly in every case

quiz.q: What must be defined before running a chi-squared goodness-of-fit test?
options: The physical location where data was collected
The expected frequencies under a stated hypothesis
The derivative of the data set
The exact colour of the data visualization

quiz.q: In which field is the chi-squared goodness-of-fit test commonly applied?
options: Translating a text between languages
Analyzing survey or experimental data across categories
Designing architectural blueprints
Composing musical scales

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: The Physics of Rainbows and Light Dispersion
subjects.summary: Grade 8 Science strand: rainbows form when sunlight is refracted, reflected, and dispersed by water droplets in the air, splitting white light into its full spectrum of colours.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: The Physics of Rainbows and Light Dispersion

quiz.q: What causes a rainbow to form?
options: Wind blowing dust into the air
Sunlight passing through solid glass only
Sound waves bending around clouds
Sunlight being refracted, reflected, and dispersed by water droplets

quiz.q: What is light dispersion?
options: The complete disappearance of light
The splitting of white light into its full spectrum of colours
The merging of colours into black
The blocking of all light entirely

quiz.q: What does a water droplet do to sunlight to create a rainbow?
options: Turns light into sound
Refracts and reflects it, separating the colours
Absorbs all light with no reflection
Blocks light completely

quiz.q: What is the correct order of colours typically seen in a rainbow?
options: Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet
Random colours with no pattern
Black, white, grey, and brown only
Only red and blue

quiz.q: Why can rainbows sometimes be seen after rain on a sunny day?
options: Rainbows require no water at all
Sunlight interacts with remaining water droplets in the air
Rainbows only form underwater
Rainbows only occur at night

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: The National Housing Act of 1938
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: the National Housing Act of 1938 expanded federal involvement in housing by offering government-backed loans to encourage home construction and repair during the Great Depression, laying groundwork for later federal housing policy in Canada.

quiz.q: In what year was the National Housing Act passed?
What did the National Housing Act offer to encourage home construction?
options: Mandatory military service for builders
Free land grants to every citizen
A new national currency
Government-backed loans

quiz.q: During what economic period was the National Housing Act introduced?
options: The height of the Klondike Gold Rush
The Great Depression
The years immediately following Confederation
The dot-com boom of the 1990s

quiz.q: What broader policy area did the National Housing Act help establish?
options: Federal involvement in housing policy
A national system of criminal courts
A national postal service
Federal control over provincial elections

quiz.q: Why might a government offer backed loans for housing during a depression?
options: To discourage any new construction during hard times
To eliminate the need for any future housing
To stimulate construction activity and employment during an economic downturn
To transfer all housing responsibility to foreign governments

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Writing: The Business Memo and Professional Email
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: a business memo or professional email is a concise workplace document that communicates information, requests, or decisions to colleagues using a clear subject line, direct opening statement, and organized body, avoiding unnecessary detail.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a business memo or professional email?
options: To communicate information, requests, or decisions to colleagues concisely
To replace all verbal communication in a workplace permanently
To entertain readers with an extended work of fiction
To provide a lengthy personal narrative unrelated to work

quiz.q: What should a professional email typically include at the top?
options: An unrelated image with no context
A blank space with no information
A handwritten signature only
A clear subject line

quiz.q: How should the opening of a business memo generally be structured?
options: With a long personal anecdote unrelated to the topic
With a detailed weather report
With a direct statement of the main point or request
With no information about the purpose of the memo

quiz.q: Why do business memos favour concise, organized writing?
options: Because concise writing has no value in a professional setting
Because memos are never read by anyone
Because organization makes information harder to find
Because workplace readers often need to find key information quickly

quiz.q: Which of the following is appropriate content for a professional email?
options: A message written entirely in informal slang
An unrelated joke with no connection to work
A clearly stated request with any necessary supporting details
A vague message with no clear purpose

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Calculus: LHopitals Rule for Evaluating Limits
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: LHopitals Rule provides a method for evaluating limits that produce an indeterminate form such as zero over zero, by taking the derivative of the numerator and denominator separately and then re-evaluating the resulting limit.

quiz.q: What type of limit is LHopitals Rule designed to evaluate?
options: A limit that only involves constant functions
A limit that cannot be expressed as a fraction of any kind
A limit that produces an indeterminate form such as zero over zero
A limit that is already a whole number with no calculation needed

quiz.q: What is the general procedure used in LHopitals Rule?
options: Taking the derivative of the numerator and denominator separately, then re-evaluating the limit
Ignoring the denominator entirely
Multiplying the numerator and denominator by zero
Replacing the entire limit with an arbitrary constant

quiz.q: What must be true about a limit before LHopitals Rule can be applied?
options: It must already have a defined finite value
It must be evaluated at exactly zero
It must involve only whole numbers
It must result in an indeterminate form

quiz.q: Why might LHopitals Rule need to be applied more than once to a single limit?
options: Applying it twice always produces an incorrect answer
LHopitals Rule can never be applied more than once under any circumstance
The resulting limit after one application may still be an indeterminate form
The rule only works when applied exactly three times

quiz.q: LHopitals Rule builds most directly on which earlier calculus concept?
options: The Pythagorean Theorem
Basic arithmetic with no calculus involved
The quadratic formula
Derivatives

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Earth Science: Earthquakes and Seismology
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand: seismology is the scientific study of earthquakes, which occur when built-up stress along a fault is suddenly released, sending seismic waves through the Earth that scientists measure using instruments called seismographs.

quiz.q: What is seismology the study of?
options: Earthquakes and the seismic waves they produce
The life cycle of stars
The formation of clouds and weather patterns
The chemical composition of ocean water

quiz.q: What causes an earthquake to occur?
options: The gradual erosion of a river bank
A sudden drop in atmospheric temperature
Built-up stress along a fault is suddenly released
A change in the phase of the moon

quiz.q: What instrument do scientists use to measure seismic waves?
options: A barometer
A thermometer
A spectrometer
A seismograph

quiz.q: What travels through the Earth during an earthquake?
options: Light waves through solid rock
Sound waves through the atmosphere only
Seismic waves
Radio waves generated by the fault line

quiz.q: Why do earthquakes tend to occur more frequently along fault lines?
options: Fault lines have no connection to tectonic activity
Earthquakes occur with equal frequency everywhere on Earth
Fault lines only exist in areas with no tectonic plates
Stress accumulates most readily where tectonic plates meet and grind against each other

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: The Munich Agreement and Canadas Response, 1938
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: the Munich Agreement of 1938 allowed Nazi Germany to annex the Sudetenland region of Czechoslovakia in exchange for a promise to seek no further territorial expansion, a policy of appeasement that Prime Minister Mackenzie King publicly supported at the time.

quiz.q: In what year was the Munich Agreement signed?
What territory did the Munich Agreement allow Nazi Germany to annex?
options: A territory belonging to the United States
The entire nation of Poland
A province of Canada
The Sudetenland region of Czechoslovakia

quiz.q: What policy did the Munich Agreement represent?
options: Unconditional surrender
Outright military confrontation
Complete economic isolation
Appeasement

quiz.q: What promise did Germany make as part of the Munich Agreement?
options: To join the League of Nations
To grant independence to all of its territories
To seek no further territorial expansion
To immediately disarm its entire military

quiz.q: How did Prime Minister Mackenzie King respond to the Munich Agreement at the time?
options: He immediately declared war in response
He publicly supported it
He resigned from office in protest
He refused to comment on international affairs

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Grammar: Conditional Sentences and Subjunctive Mood
subjects.summary: Grade 8 Language strand: conditional sentences express a condition and its result using if-clauses, and the subjunctive mood expresses wishes, hypothetical situations, or statements contrary to fact.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Grammar: Conditional Sentences and Subjunctive Mood

quiz.q: A conditional sentence expresses ___.
options: A statement with no possible condition attached
A concept unrelated to conditional sentences
A command with no connection to any condition
A condition and its result, often using an if-clause

quiz.q: The subjunctive mood is used to express ___.
options: A concept unrelated to the subjunctive mood
Wishes, hypothetical situations, or statements contrary to fact
Only statements that are completely factual and certain
Commands given directly to another person

quiz.q: Which sentence correctly uses the subjunctive mood?
options: If I am taller, I would join the team.
If I were taller, I would join the team.
A sentence unrelated to the subjunctive mood
If I was taller, I would join the team.

quiz.q: In the sentence “If it rains, we will cancel the picnic,” the if-clause states ___.
options: A concept unrelated to conditional sentences
The result of an already completed action
The condition that must occur for the result to happen
A wish that is impossible to fulfil

quiz.q: Why is understanding conditional sentences useful in formal writing?
options: Every sentence must contain a conditional clause
Conditional sentences have no real use in formal writing
A reason unrelated to grammar

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Geometry: Fractals and Self-Similarity
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: a fractal is a geometric figure that displays self-similarity, meaning smaller portions of the figure resemble the whole shape at different scales, a property found in mathematical constructions as well as natural forms like coastlines and snowflakes.

quiz.q: What key property defines a fractal?
options: A shape that only exists in three dimensions
Self-similarity, where smaller portions resemble the whole shape at different scales
A shape with exactly three straight sides
A number with no decimal component

quiz.q: What does self-similarity mean in the context of fractals?
options: A shape becomes a perfect circle when zoomed in
Every fractal is identical to every other fractal
Smaller sections of a shape look similar to the entire shape
A shape has no repeating pattern at any scale

quiz.q: Which of the following is a natural example often associated with fractal-like patterns?
options: A coastline
A single straight line segment
A perfectly smooth sphere
A flat, featureless plane

quiz.q: How does zooming into a fractal typically appear?
options: Similar patterns continue to appear at smaller and smaller scales
The shape disappears entirely after one level of zoom
The shape transforms into an entirely unrelated image
The shape becomes completely blank with no detail

quiz.q: Why are fractals of interest beyond pure mathematics?
options: They were disproven and are no longer studied
They can only describe perfectly regular polygons
They have no application outside of abstract theory
They help describe complex natural patterns that simple Euclidean shapes cannot easily capture

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Genetic Engineering in Agriculture: An Introduction to GMOs
subjects.summary: Grade 8 Science strand: genetically modified organisms, or GMOs, are created by altering an organisms DNA to introduce desirable traits, such as pest resistance or improved crop yield, in modern agriculture.
subjects.resourceLabel: YouTube: Genetic Engineering in Agriculture: An Introduction to GMOs

quiz.q: What does GMO stand for?
options: Green modified oxygen
Growth management order
Generally moved organism
Genetically modified organism

quiz.q: How are GMOs created?
options: By changing the organisms diet with no genetic change
By exposing the organism to sunlight only
By freezing the organism permanently
By altering an organisms DNA to introduce desirable traits

quiz.q: What is one reason crops might be genetically modified?
options: To eliminate the need for farming entirely
To improve pest resistance or crop yield
To make the crop completely inedible
To remove all genetic material from the plant

quiz.q: Why is genetic engineering in agriculture a topic of ongoing debate?
options: GMOs have no effect on agriculture at all
The topic has no scientific basis
People have different views on its safety, ethics, and environmental impact
Everyone agrees completely on every aspect of GMOs

quiz.q: Genetic engineering in agriculture is an application of which broader scientific field?
options: Biotechnology
Geology
Astronomy
Meteorology

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: The Founding of Trans-Canada Air Lines in 1937
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: Trans-Canada Air Lines was founded in 1937 as a federal Crown corporation to establish reliable, government-backed commercial air travel across the country, later becoming Air Canada and shaping the development of Canadian aviation infrastructure.

quiz.q: In what year was Trans-Canada Air Lines founded?

options: A federal Crown corporation
A provincial ministry with no national reach
A privately owned foreign company
A volunteer-run charitable organization

quiz.q: What was the main purpose of founding Trans-Canada Air Lines?
options: To establish reliable, government-backed commercial air travel across the country
To build a network of national highways

quiz.q: What airline did Trans-Canada Air Lines eventually become?
options: The Canadian Pacific Railway
The National Film Board
The Royal Canadian Air Force
Air Canada

options: To ensure the development of national air travel infrastructure across a vast country
