quiz.q: What does a travel narrative typically recount?
options: A single event that occurs entirely at home
A purely fictional world with no real setting
A scientific report with no narrative elements
A journey to an unfamiliar location

quiz.q: What technique helps a travel narrative create a strong sense of place?
options: A list of unrelated statistics
A formal legal argument
A complete absence of any description
Vivid sensory detail

quiz.q: What might a travel narrative reflect on beyond simply describing a location?
options: A weather report with no personal reflection
The exact price of every meal purchased during the trip
How the experience of travel changed the writers perspective or understanding
A set of directions with no descriptive language

quiz.q: Why might sensory detail such as sound and smell be especially important in a travel narrative?
options: Sensory detail is never included in travel writing
It replaces the need for any narrative structure at all
It has no effect on how a reader imagines a setting
It helps immerse the reader in an unfamiliar setting they have not personally experienced

quiz.q: What distinguishes a travel narrative from a simple itinerary?
options: An itinerary always includes personal reflection
A travel narrative includes reflection and descriptive storytelling, not just a list of locations and times
There is no meaningful difference between the two forms
A travel narrative never mentions any specific location

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Algebra: Solving Rational Inequalities
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: solving a rational inequality involves finding the values of the variable that make a fraction containing that variable positive, negative, zero, or undefined, typically by identifying critical values and testing the sign of the expression across the intervals they create.

quiz.q: What does solving a rational inequality involve finding?
options: The exact single value that makes the fraction equal to one
The values of the variable that satisfy a given inequality involving a fraction
The colour used to graph the inequality
The name of the variable used in the expression

quiz.q: What are critical values in the context of a rational inequality?
options: Values where the numerator or denominator equals zero
Values that make every rational inequality false
Any value chosen at random with no mathematical basis
Values that cannot be graphed on a number line

quiz.q: Why must values that make the denominator of a rational inequality equal to zero be excluded?
options: Zero denominators always produce a true inequality
Division by zero is undefined
Those values always satisfy the inequality
Excluding values has no mathematical purpose

quiz.q: What is a common method for testing the sign of a rational expression across an interval?
options: Only testing the endpoints of the entire number line
Assuming every interval has the same sign with no testing
Substituting a test value from each interval into the expression
Ignoring the denominator entirely

quiz.q: How is the solution to a rational inequality typically expressed?
options: As a single word with no numerical value
As a set of intervals on a number line
As an equation set equal to zero only
As a single fixed number with no range

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Earth Science: Sand Dunes and Aeolian Landforms
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand: sand dunes are aeolian landforms shaped by wind erosion and deposition, forming when wind transports and accumulates loose sand grains around an obstacle or over time, with dune shape influenced by wind direction, sand supply, and vegetation cover.

quiz.q: What are sand dunes an example of?
options: Landforms shaped entirely by ocean currents
Landforms created by glacial ice alone
Aeolian landforms shaped by wind
Landforms formed only by volcanic eruptions

quiz.q: What process causes sand to accumulate into a dune?
options: Sand grains being magnetically attracted to one another
A sudden drop in air temperature
Sand grains chemically bonding together instantly
Wind transporting and depositing loose sand grains

quiz.q: What factor can influence the shape of a sand dune?
options: The number of animals living nearby
The exact colour of the surrounding rock
Wind direction, sand supply, and vegetation cover
The phase of the moon on a given night

quiz.q: What term describes processes shaped primarily by wind?
options: Aeolian
Fluvial
Volcanic
Glacial

quiz.q: Why can vegetation help stabilize a sand dune?
options: Plant roots can anchor sand grains and reduce further wind erosion
Plants prevent wind from blowing across a dune entirely
Vegetation always increases the rate of wind erosion
Vegetation has no physical effect on loose sand

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: Indigenous Peoples and the Extension of the Federal Vote in 1960
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: in 1960, the Diefenbaker government extended the federal vote to First Nations peoples living on reserves without requiring them to give up their status or treaty rights, ending a long-standing restriction and marking a step toward greater political inclusion, though many barriers to full equality remained.

quiz.q: What change did the federal government make in 1960 regarding First Nations peoples?
options: It ended all federal elections in Canada
It extended the federal vote to First Nations peoples living on reserves
It removed the right to vote from all Canadian citizens
It created an entirely new federal electoral system

quiz.q: What did First Nations voters not have to give up in order to vote after 1960?
options: Their right to live in Canada
Their right to own property
Their citizenship in Canada
Their status or treaty rights

quiz.q: Which government extended the federal vote to First Nations peoples in 1960?
options: The Mackenzie King government
The Trudeau government
The Diefenbaker government
The Laurier government

quiz.q: What long-standing restriction did the 1960 change end?
options: A restriction on attending public school
A restriction on international travel for all Canadians
A restriction that had prevented many First Nations peoples from voting in federal elections
A restriction on owning a business in Canada

quiz.q: What remained true even after the 1960 change was made?
options: All inequality faced by Indigenous peoples in Canada ended immediately
No further historical change affecting Indigenous rights ever occurred
Indigenous peoples gained full political equality with no further issues
Many barriers to full equality for Indigenous peoples remained

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Media Literacy: Analyzing Sports Broadcasting and Commentary
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: sports broadcasting combines live play-by-play description with colour commentary that adds context, opinion, and analysis, shaping how an audience interprets a game through word choice, tone, and the narratives commentators choose to emphasize.

quiz.q: What does play-by-play description provide during a sports broadcast?
options: A prerecorded segment unrelated to the live game
A written summary published only after the event ends
A silent broadcast with no spoken description
A live account of the action as it happens

quiz.q: What does colour commentary typically add to a sports broadcast?
options: Context, opinion, and analysis
An unrelated news segment about world events
A completely silent broadcast
A recipe segment with no connection to sports

quiz.q: How can commentators shape audience interpretation of a game?
options: By reading directly from an unrelated script with no analysis
Through word choice, tone, and the narratives they choose to emphasize
By remaining completely silent throughout the broadcast
Commentary has no influence on how an audience understands a game

quiz.q: Why might media literacy be useful when watching a sports broadcast?
options: It helps viewers recognize bias or a particular narrative within the commentary
It proves that sports broadcasts contain no spoken language
It guarantees that all commentary is entirely free of opinion
It removes the need to think critically about broadcast content

quiz.q: Which of the following is an example of colour commentary rather than play-by-play?
options: A direct description of a ball crossing the goal line
A statement of the current score with no further comment
An analysis of why a team changed strategy at halftime
The time remaining on the game clock

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Discrete Math: Eulerian and Hamiltonian Paths
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: an Eulerian path visits every edge of a graph exactly once, while a Hamiltonian path visits every vertex of a graph exactly once, two related but distinct concepts used to model routing problems such as delivery routes and circuit design.

quiz.q: What must an Eulerian path visit exactly once?
options: Every edge of a graph
Every colour used to draw a graph
Every possible graph that could ever exist
The exact midpoint of a graph

quiz.q: What must a Hamiltonian path visit exactly once?
options: Every edge of a graph
Only the starting vertex of a graph
No vertices or edges at all
Every vertex of a graph

quiz.q: How do Eulerian and Hamiltonian paths differ from one another?
options: An Eulerian path focuses on edges, while a Hamiltonian path focuses on vertices
They are identical concepts with different names
An Eulerian path can never be drawn on any graph
A Hamiltonian path must always repeat every edge twice

quiz.q: Which real-world problem could be modelled using a Hamiltonian path?
options: Finding the area under a curve
Measuring the exact temperature of a room
Calculating the derivative of a polynomial function
Planning a delivery route that visits every location exactly once

quiz.q: Why are Eulerian and Hamiltonian paths useful in fields such as logistics and circuit design?
options: They eliminate the need for any planning in routing problems
They only apply to graphs with a single vertex
They provide mathematical models for efficiently visiting locations or connections without unnecessary repetition
They have no practical application outside of pure mathematics

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Biology: The Human Liver and Detoxification
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand: the liver is a vital organ that filters blood from the digestive tract, breaking down toxins, metabolizing nutrients, and producing bile to aid digestion, making it central to maintaining chemical balance within the body.

quiz.q: What is one of the main functions of the liver?
options: Pumping blood throughout the entire body
Regulating body temperature directly through the skin
Filtering blood and breaking down toxins
Producing sound for the vocal cords

quiz.q: What substance does the liver produce to aid digestion?
options: Bile
Insulin
Saliva
Mucus

quiz.q: From where does the liver receive blood rich in absorbed nutrients?
options: The digestive tract
The skin exclusively
The bones exclusively
The lungs exclusively

quiz.q: What role does the liver play in metabolizing nutrients?
options: It destroys all nutrients before they can be used
It only processes nutrients that enter through the skin
It has no involvement in nutrient processing at all
It processes nutrients absorbed from digestion so they can be used or stored by the body

quiz.q: Why is the liver considered central to maintaining chemical balance in the body?
options: It exclusively controls eye colour
It has no connection to any chemical process in the body
It filters toxins and regulates many substances circulating in the blood
It only affects the colour of a persons hair

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: The Diefenbaker Government and the Nuclear Weapons Controversy
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: the Diefenbaker government faced a bitter controversy in the early 1960s over whether Canada should accept nuclear warheads for the Bomarc missiles and other weapons systems already stationed on Canadian soil, a dispute that divided the cabinet and contributed to the governments defeat in 1963.

quiz.q: What controversy did the Diefenbaker government face in the early 1960s?
options: Whether Canada should accept nuclear warheads for weapons systems already on Canadian soil
Whether Canada should abolish the Senate
Whether Canada should join the United Nations
Whether Canada should adopt a new currency

quiz.q: Which missile system was at the centre of the nuclear weapons controversy?
options: The Sputnik satellite
The V-2 rocket
The Bomarc missile
The Avro Arrow

quiz.q: How did the nuclear weapons controversy affect the Diefenbaker cabinet?
options: It had no effect on the cabinet at all
It caused the cabinet to unanimously support the warheads immediately
It divided the cabinet over whether to accept the warheads
It led to the permanent cancellation of the cabinet

quiz.q: What political outcome did the controversy contribute to?
options: A formal merger of Canada with another country
The permanent end of federal elections in Canada
An immediate landslide re-election for Diefenbaker
The defeat of the Diefenbaker government in 1963

quiz.q: What broader Cold War tension formed the backdrop of this controversy?
options: Debates over nuclear weapons and defence alliances between Western nations
A disagreement over provincial highway funding
A trade agreement with a South American country
A dispute over Arctic fishing rights

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Literature: The Detective and Mystery Genre
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: the detective and mystery genre centres on solving a crime or puzzle through the careful gathering of clues and logical deduction, typically following an investigator who must interpret evidence more skillfully than the reader to reach the correct solution.

quiz.q: What does the detective and mystery genre typically centre on?
options: A purely descriptive account of a setting with no plot
A story with no conflict or problem to solve
Solving a crime or puzzle through the gathering of clues and logical deduction
A collection of unrelated poems with no narrative

quiz.q: What skill does a detective typically use to reach a solution?
options: Logical deduction based on interpreting evidence
Random guessing with no basis in evidence
Ignoring all clues presented in the story
Refusing to investigate any aspect of the crime

quiz.q: What is a defining feature of many detective narratives?
options: No evidence is ever presented to the reader
The identity of the culprit is revealed in the first sentence
The investigator interprets evidence more skillfully than the reader
The crime is solved before the story begins

quiz.q: Why do readers often enjoy the mystery genre?
options: It never reveals a solution of any kind
It invites them to piece together clues alongside the investigator
It removes any sense of curiosity from the reading experience
It provides no puzzle or problem to engage with

quiz.q: Which of the following is a common element found in detective fiction?
options: A red herring intended to mislead the investigator and reader
A recipe with no connection to any crime
A weather report with no narrative purpose
A bibliography with no story elements

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Statistics: The F-Distribution and Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: analysis of variance, or ANOVA, uses the F-distribution to test whether the means of three or more groups differ significantly, comparing the variation between group means to the variation within each group to determine whether the differences are likely due to chance.

quiz.q: What does analysis of variance, or ANOVA, test?
options: The area under a single point on a graph
Whether the means of three or more groups differ significantly
The exact slope of a straight line
Whether a single number is prime

quiz.q: What distribution does ANOVA rely on to determine significance?
options: The F-distribution
The Poisson distribution
The binomial distribution
The geometric distribution

quiz.q: What two types of variation does ANOVA compare?
options: Variation between group means and variation within each group
The alphabetical order of group names
The colour of each group and its exact size
The physical location where each group was measured

quiz.q: Why is ANOVA useful when comparing more than two groups at once?
options: It eliminates the need for any data collection
It can only be used to compare exactly two groups
It tests all group means simultaneously rather than requiring many separate pairwise tests
It guarantees that all group means are always identical

quiz.q: What might a large F-value in an ANOVA test suggest?
options: That no data was collected for the study
That the differences between group means are unlikely to be due to chance alone
That the study contains no groups at all
That every group mean is exactly equal

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Physics: Lenses and Image Formation
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand: a lens is a transparent optical device that refracts light to form an image, with a converging lens bending light rays toward a focal point and a diverging lens spreading light rays apart, producing images that vary in size, orientation, and position depending on the lens type and object distance.

quiz.q: What does a lens do to light passing through it?
options: Reflects all light back toward its source
Refracts the light to form an image
Converts light into sound waves
Absorbs all light with no image produced

quiz.q: What does a converging lens do to light rays?
options: Bends them toward a focal point
Blocks them from passing through entirely
Spreads them apart in every direction
Has no effect on light rays at all

quiz.q: What does a diverging lens do to light rays?
options: Absorbs them completely
Spreads them apart
Converts them into a different colour
Bends them toward a single focal point

quiz.q: What factors can affect the size, orientation, and position of an image formed by a lens?
options: The type of lens and the distance of the object from the lens
The brand name of the lens
The colour of the lens frame
The time of day the lens is used

quiz.q: Which everyday device relies on lenses to form an image?
options: A thermometer
A battery
A speaker
A camera

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: The 1963 Federal Election and the Return of the Liberals Under Pearson
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: the 1963 federal election returned the Liberal Party to power under Lester Pearson, forming a minority government after the Diefenbaker Progressive Conservatives were weakened by internal divisions and the fallout from the nuclear weapons controversy.

quiz.q: Which party returned to power in the 1963 federal election?
options: The Progressive Conservatives, under John Diefenbaker
The Liberal Party, under Lester Pearson
The Reform Party
The Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

quiz.q: What type of government did Pearson form after the 1963 election?
options: A minority government
A government with every seat in the House of Commons
A government formed entirely of independent members
No government was formed at all

quiz.q: What weakened the Progressive Conservatives heading into the 1963 election?
options: An agreement to cancel all future elections
Internal divisions and fallout from the nuclear weapons controversy
A sudden and total collapse of the federal government structure
A complete absence of any political party in Canada

quiz.q: Who led the Liberal Party to victory in the 1963 election?
options: John Diefenbaker
Lester Pearson
Louis St. Laurent
Pierre Trudeau

quiz.q: What broader period of Canadian politics did the 1963 election help usher in?
options: A period with no elected government of any kind
The end of the Canadian parliamentary system
The Pearson era of minority Liberal governments
The permanent dominance of a single political party with no opposition

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Oral Communication: Nonverbal Communication and Body Language
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: nonverbal communication includes body language such as posture, gestures, facial expression, and eye contact, all of which can reinforce, contradict, or add nuance to the words a speaker uses during a presentation or conversation.

quiz.q: What does nonverbal communication include?
options: A single printed document with no live speaker
Body language such as posture, gestures, facial expression, and eye contact
A written transcript with no spoken element
Only the exact words spoken during a conversation

quiz.q: How can body language relate to spoken words during a presentation?
options: It has no relationship to spoken words whatsoever
It completely replaces the need for any spoken words
It always contradicts spoken words with no exception
It can reinforce, contradict, or add nuance to what is being said

quiz.q: Why might a speaker maintain eye contact during a conversation?
options: To convey confidence and engagement with the listener
To avoid communicating with the listener entirely
Because eye contact has no effect on communication
To signal that the conversation has ended

quiz.q: What might crossed arms and a lack of eye contact suggest about a speaker during a conversation?
options: Nothing at all, since body language carries no meaning
That the speaker is about to give a formal toast
Complete enthusiasm and total engagement in every case
Discomfort or disengagement, depending on the context

quiz.q: Why is awareness of nonverbal communication useful in oral communication skills?
options: It guarantees that spoken words alone will always be understood correctly
It has no connection to effective communication of any kind
It helps a speaker align their body language with their intended message
It removes the need to ever consider an audience

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Geometry: Spherical Geometry and Great Circles
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: spherical geometry studies shapes and angles on the surface of a sphere rather than a flat plane, where the shortest path between two points is an arc of a great circle, a concept used in real-world applications such as long-distance air and sea navigation.

quiz.q: What surface does spherical geometry study?
options: A completely flat plane only
The surface of a sphere
A single straight line
A three-dimensional cube

quiz.q: What represents the shortest path between two points on a sphere?
options: A perfectly horizontal line at the equator only
An arc of a great circle
A path that ignores the curvature of the sphere
A straight line drawn through the centre of the sphere

quiz.q: What is a great circle?
options: A circle with no defined radius
A shape that is not actually circular at all
A circle on a sphere whose plane passes through the spheres centre
A circle drawn on a completely flat sheet of paper

quiz.q: In which real-world field is spherical geometry commonly applied?
options: Long-distance air and sea navigation
Balancing a chemical equation
Filing a legal document
Simplifying a rational expression

quiz.q: How do the angles of a triangle drawn on a sphere differ from those of a triangle on a flat plane?
options: Spherical triangles cannot have angles at all
The angles of a spherical triangle always sum to exactly 90 degrees
The angles of a spherical triangle can sum to more than 180 degrees
The angles always sum to exactly 180 degrees, identical to a flat triangle

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Chemistry: The Chemistry of Soap and Saponification
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand: soap is produced through saponification, a chemical reaction in which a fat or oil reacts with a strong base to form soap molecules and glycerol, with each soap molecule having a water-attracting head and a grease-attracting tail that allows it to lift oils away from a surface.

quiz.q: What chemical process produces soap?
options: Saponification
Distillation
Combustion
Electrolysis

quiz.q: What two substances react during saponification?
options: Water and table salt
A fat or oil and a strong base
Two different metals
Oxygen and hydrogen gas

quiz.q: What byproduct is formed alongside soap during saponification?
options: Carbon dioxide gas
Table sugar
Pure oxygen
Glycerol

quiz.q: What structural feature allows a soap molecule to lift grease away from a surface?
options: A single uniform charge across the entire molecule
A water-attracting head and a grease-attracting tail
An identical structure to a water molecule
A complete absence of any chemical bonds

quiz.q: Why is soaps dual structure useful for cleaning?
options: It has no effect on removing dirt or grease from a surface
It prevents soap from ever coming into contact with water
It causes soap to repel all substances equally
It allows soap to bind to both grease and water, letting grease be rinsed away

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: The Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism was established in 1963 by the Pearson government to examine the state of bilingualism in Canada and recommend measures to better reflect the countrys English and French linguistic duality, laying groundwork for the Official Languages Act.

quiz.q: When was the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism established?
Which government established the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism?
options: The Diefenbaker government
The Trudeau government
The Mackenzie King government
The Pearson government

quiz.q: What was the Royal Commission asked to examine?
options: The state of Canadian agriculture
The design of a new Canadian flag
The state of bilingualism in Canada
The condition of Canadian railways

quiz.q: What later federal legislation did the Royal Commissions work help lay the groundwork for?
options: The National Housing Act
The Canadian Bill of Rights
The Official Languages Act
The Old Age Pensions Act

quiz.q: What broader aspect of Canadian identity did the Royal Commission focus on reflecting?
options: An exclusively agricultural national economy
A single unified provincial identity with no federal role
The countrys English and French linguistic duality
A purely military national identity

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Film Study: Analyzing Editing Techniques and Montage
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: film editing shapes how a story is told by determining the order, pacing, and juxtaposition of shots, and montage is a specific editing technique that assembles a rapid sequence of images to condense time, build emotion, or suggest a relationship between ideas.

quiz.q: What does film editing shape?
options: The physical location where a film is screened
The exact colour of the actors costumes
How a story is told through the order, pacing, and juxtaposition of shots
Only the volume of the films soundtrack

quiz.q: What is montage?
options: A method of removing all sound from a film entirely
An editing technique that assembles a rapid sequence of images
A single unedited continuous shot with no cuts
A technique used only in silent films with no sound

quiz.q: What can montage help a filmmaker accomplish?
options: Remove any sense of narrative from a film
Eliminate the need for any images in a scene
Prevent the audience from experiencing any emotion
Condense time, build emotion, or suggest a relationship between ideas

quiz.q: How does the pacing of edited shots affect a viewers experience?
options: Faster cuts can create tension or excitement, while slower cuts can create calm or reflection
Pacing only affects the films runtime and nothing else
Pacing has no effect on how a viewer experiences a film
Every film uses identical pacing regardless of its content

quiz.q: Why might a filmmaker juxtapose two contrasting shots next to each other?
options: To suggest a meaningful relationship or contrast between the two images
To ensure the two shots have no connection to one another
Because juxtaposition is never used in film editing
To remove all meaning from the sequence of shots

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Algebra: The Rational Root Theorem
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: the Rational Root Theorem provides a method for identifying possible rational roots of a polynomial equation with integer coefficients by comparing the factors of the constant term to the factors of the leading coefficient, narrowing down candidates before testing them directly.

quiz.q: What does the Rational Root Theorem help identify?
options: The number of dimensions in a graph
The exact derivative of a polynomial function
The area under a polynomial curve
Possible rational roots of a polynomial equation with integer coefficients

quiz.q: What two values does the Rational Root Theorem compare?
options: The factors of the constant term and the factors of the leading coefficient
The degree of the polynomial and its y-intercept only
The exact colour and size of the graph
The number of variables and the number of constants

quiz.q: What must be true about the coefficients of a polynomial for the Rational Root Theorem to apply directly?
options: They must all be equal to zero
They must all be irrational numbers
They must be integers
They must be expressed only as percentages

quiz.q: Why is the Rational Root Theorem useful before testing candidate roots directly?
options: It narrows down a large set of possible roots to a smaller, manageable list
It proves that no polynomial can have any rational roots
It eliminates the need to ever solve a polynomial equation
It guarantees every real number is automatically a root

quiz.q: After identifying possible rational roots, what is typically done next?
options: The candidates are immediately discarded without any testing
The equation is declared unsolvable with no further steps
The polynomial is redefined to remove all of its terms
Each candidate is tested, often using substitution or synthetic division, to confirm whether it is an actual root

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Earth Science: Deltas and River Systems
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand: a river delta forms where a river slows and deposits sediment as it enters a larger body of water such as a lake or ocean, building a fan-shaped or branching landform over time and creating fertile, biologically productive habitats at the rivers mouth.

quiz.q: Where does a river delta typically form?
options: At the exact source of a river high in the mountains
Only at the bottom of a deep ocean trench
In the middle of a desert with no water present
Where a river enters a larger body of water and deposits sediment

quiz.q: Why does a river deposit sediment as it approaches a larger body of water?
options: The water instantly freezes at the rivers mouth
The river slows down, reducing its ability to carry sediment
The river suddenly speeds up and carries no sediment at all
Sediment is created only at the source of the river

quiz.q: What shape do many river deltas form over time?
options: A perfectly circular landform with no variation
A single straight line with no branching
A shape identical to a mountain peak
A fan-shaped or branching landform

quiz.q: Why are deltas often biologically productive habitats?
options: Deltas contain no nutrients of any kind
Deltas are always too dry to support any living organisms
Delta sediment actively repels all forms of life
The fertile sediment and nutrient-rich water support a wide range of plant and animal life

quiz.q: Which factor can affect how quickly a delta forms and grows?
options: The exact number of animals living nearby
The amount of sediment carried by the river
The name given to the river by local residents
The colour of the surrounding rock

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: The Great Flag Debate and the Adoption of the Maple Leaf in 1964
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: the Great Flag Debate was a lengthy and often contentious parliamentary dispute in 1964 over adopting a new, distinctly Canadian national flag to replace the Red Ensign, resolved when the maple leaf design proposed by Lester Pearson was adopted, with the new flag raised for the first time in February 1965.

quiz.q: What was the Great Flag Debate about?
options: Selecting a new national capital city
Adopting a new, distinctly Canadian national flag
Adopting a new national currency
Choosing a new national anthem

quiz.q: What flag did the new Canadian flag replace?
options: The Red Ensign
The Union Jack of the United Kingdom
The flag of the United States
The flag of France

quiz.q: In what year did the Great Flag Debate take place in Parliament?
Who proposed the maple leaf design ultimately adopted as the new flag?
options: Prime Minister Lester Pearson
Prime Minister Louis St. Laurent
Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau
Prime Minister John Diefenbaker

quiz.q: When was the new Canadian flag first raised?
options: February 1965
January 1947
September 1939
July 1867

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Grammar: Sentence Combining and Coordination Strategies
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: sentence combining joins two or more short, related sentences into a single, more sophisticated sentence using coordination strategies such as coordinating conjunctions, semicolons, or subordinating structures, improving flow and reducing choppy, repetitive writing.

quiz.q: What does sentence combining do?
options: Splits one long sentence into many unrelated sentences
Joins two or more short, related sentences into a single, more sophisticated sentence
Removes all punctuation from a paragraph
Deletes the subject of every sentence in a paragraph

quiz.q: What is one strategy used in sentence combining?
options: Writing every sentence in a completely different language
Removing every verb from a sentence
Ending every sentence with a question mark regardless of content
Using a coordinating conjunction to join related ideas

quiz.q: What problem in writing can sentence combining help reduce?
options: A total lack of subjects and verbs
Choppy, repetitive writing made up of many short sentences
Overly long paragraphs with no sentences at all
A complete absence of any punctuation

quiz.q: Which example demonstrates effective sentence combining?
options: The rain stopped, and the sun came out.
Rain the stopped sun the out came.
The rain stopped. The sun came out.
Stopped rain sun came out.

quiz.q: Why might a writer use varied sentence combining strategies throughout a piece of writing?
options: To eliminate all coordinating conjunctions from the text
Because sentence combining always makes writing less clear
To make every sentence identical in length and structure
To create more natural flow and avoid a repetitive, monotonous rhythm

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Calculus: Antiderivatives and the Indefinite Integral
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: an antiderivative of a function is a new function whose derivative equals the original function, and the indefinite integral represents the entire family of antiderivatives of a function, differing from one another only by a constant of integration.

quiz.q: What is an antiderivative of a function?
options: The exact same function written in a different colour
A function that has no derivative at all
A new function whose derivative equals the original function
A function with no relationship to the original function

quiz.q: What does the indefinite integral of a function represent?
options: A single specific numerical value only
A function with no connection to derivatives
The entire family of antiderivatives of that function
The area under a curve between two fixed points only

quiz.q: What distinguishes different antiderivatives of the same function from one another?
options: A constant of integration
The colour used to graph the function
The degree of the original polynomial
The variable used in the original function

quiz.q: Why is a constant of integration included when writing an indefinite integral?
options: Because the derivative of any constant is zero, so many antiderivatives are possible
Because indefinite integrals cannot include any constant
Because integration always produces a negative number
Because every antiderivative must equal exactly zero

quiz.q: How is antidifferentiation related to differentiation?
options: It is completely unrelated to differentiation
It can only be applied to constant functions
It always produces the same result as differentiation
It is the reverse process of differentiation

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Biology: Fish Migration and Life Cycles: The Salmon Run
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand: many salmon species hatch in freshwater streams, migrate to the ocean to mature, and then return to the same freshwater stream where they hatched to spawn, a demanding life cycle known as the salmon run that plays a vital ecological role in many Canadian watersheds.

quiz.q: Where do many salmon species hatch?
options: In freshwater streams
In freshwater lakes located in deserts
In the deep open ocean
On dry land with no water present

quiz.q: Where do salmon typically migrate to mature after hatching?
options: The ocean
A landlocked desert with no water
An underground cave system
A mountain summit with no water source

quiz.q: What do adult salmon typically do when they are ready to spawn?
options: Stop reproducing entirely once they reach adulthood
Remain permanently in the ocean with no further migration
Return to the same freshwater stream where they hatched
Migrate to a completely unrelated species habitat

quiz.q: What term describes this demanding migratory life cycle of salmon?
options: The salmon run
The hibernation cycle
The photosynthetic cycle
The predator cycle

quiz.q: Why is the salmon run considered ecologically important in many Canadian watersheds?
options: It transports nutrients between ocean and freshwater ecosystems and supports many other species
It removes all nutrients permanently from the watershed
It only affects a single unrelated species with no broader impact
It has no effect on any other species in the ecosystem

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: The Company of Young Canadians and Youth Activism in the 1960s
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: the Company of Young Canadians was a federally funded volunteer organization created in 1966 to engage young Canadians in community development and social change projects, reflecting a broader wave of youth activism and social movements that characterized Canada and much of the world during the 1960s.

quiz.q: What was the Company of Young Canadians?
options: A federal department overseeing international trade
A private corporation focused entirely on manufacturing
A federally funded volunteer organization created to engage young Canadians in community development
A branch of the Canadian military created for youth recruits

quiz.q: In what year was the Company of Young Canadians created?
What type of projects did the Company of Young Canadians focus on?
options: Railway construction projects only
Military training exercises only
International banking regulations
Community development and social change projects

quiz.q: What broader trend did the Company of Young Canadians reflect during the 1960s?
options: A decline in community organizations across Canada
A wave of youth activism and social movements
A complete absence of youth involvement in public life
A nationwide ban on volunteer work

quiz.q: How did youth activism in 1960s Canada relate to trends elsewhere in the world?
options: It had no connection whatsoever to international events
It occurred in complete isolation from any global trend
It was the only example of youth activism in world history
It reflected a broader wave of youth activism occurring in many countries during the decade

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Writing: The Product Review and Consumer Persuasion
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: a product review evaluates the features, quality, and value of a product for potential consumers, combining descriptive detail with persuasive language to help readers decide whether the product is worth purchasing.

quiz.q: What does a product review evaluate?
options: A completely fictional story with no real product involved
A scientific theory unrelated to consumer goods
The features, quality, and value of a product for potential consumers
A historical event with no connection to any product

quiz.q: What two elements does a product review typically combine?
options: A recipe and a musical score
A map and a set of driving directions
A legal contract and a weather report
Descriptive detail and persuasive language

quiz.q: What is the purpose of persuasive language within a product review?
options: To ensure the review contains no descriptive detail
To help readers decide whether the product is worth purchasing
To remove any opinion from the review entirely
To confuse the reader about the products features

quiz.q: Which of the following would likely appear in a well-written product review?
options: A list of random numbers with no context
A specific comparison of the products strengths and weaknesses
A description of an unrelated historical event
A summary of a different, unrelated product category

quiz.q: Why might a reader consult a product review before making a purchase?
options: Because product reviews never contain any useful information
To gain insight into the products quality and value from someone who has used it
Because product reviews are legally required reading before any purchase
To avoid learning anything about the product at all

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Probability: The Law of Large Numbers
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: the law of large numbers states that as the number of trials in a random experiment increases, the experimental probability of an outcome tends to converge toward its theoretical probability, explaining why large samples tend to produce more reliable estimates than small ones.

quiz.q: What does the law of large numbers describe?
options: How experimental probability converges toward theoretical probability as trials increase
A method for calculating the exact area of a triangle
A rule stating that every event has an equal chance of occurring
A law that applies only to numbers greater than one million

quiz.q: What happens to experimental probability as the number of trials in an experiment increases?
options: It always becomes completely random with no pattern
It becomes impossible to calculate at all
It tends to converge toward the theoretical probability
It moves further away from the theoretical probability with every trial

quiz.q: Why do large samples tend to produce more reliable estimates than small samples?
options: Random fluctuations tend to average out over a greater number of trials
Small samples always produce more accurate results than large samples
Large samples always eliminate the need for any probability calculation
Sample size has no effect on the reliability of an estimate

quiz.q: Which scenario illustrates the law of large numbers?
options: Calculating the area of a circle with a given radius
Rolling a die without recording any outcome at all
Flipping a coin exactly one time and recording the result
Flipping a coin many times and observing the proportion of heads approach one half

quiz.q: Why is the law of large numbers relevant to fields such as insurance and gambling?
options: It only applies to a single trial and no more
It guarantees an individual outcome with complete certainty every time
It helps explain why outcomes become more predictable in aggregate over many repeated trials
It has no relevance to any real-world application

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Chemistry: The Chemistry of Fermentation and Brewing
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand: fermentation is a chemical process in which microorganisms such as yeast convert sugars into other compounds, such as alcohol and carbon dioxide, in the absence of oxygen, a reaction that underlies brewing, baking, and other food production processes.

quiz.q: What is fermentation?
options: A physical process with no chemical change of any kind
A chemical process in which microorganisms convert sugars into other compounds
A process that only occurs at extremely high temperatures with no microorganisms involved
A process that requires large amounts of oxygen to occur

quiz.q: Which organism commonly drives the fermentation process in brewing?
options: A type of coral
A species of large mammal
Yeast
A species of bird

quiz.q: What two compounds are commonly produced when yeast ferments sugar?
options: Iron and copper
Table salt and pure water
Alcohol and carbon dioxide
Oxygen gas and nitrogen gas

quiz.q: Under what condition does fermentation typically occur?
options: Only at freezing temperatures
In the absence of oxygen
Only inside a sealed metal container with no biological activity
Only in the presence of large amounts of oxygen

quiz.q: Which food production process relies on fermentation besides brewing?
options: Baking bread, which relies on carbon dioxide produced by yeast
Cutting fruit into smaller pieces
Freezing vegetables with no chemical change
Boiling water with no other ingredients

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: Expo 67 and the Centennial Celebrations of Canadian Confederation
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: Expo 67 was a world exposition held in Montreal in 1967 as the centrepiece of Canadas centennial celebrations marking one hundred years since Confederation, drawing tens of millions of visitors and becoming a widely remembered symbol of Canadian confidence and international engagement during the era.

quiz.q: What was Expo 67?
options: A new branch of the Canadian military
A world exposition held in Montreal in 1967
A federal election held across Canada
A treaty signed between Canada and France

quiz.q: What milestone did Expo 67 help celebrate?
options: One hundred years since Canadian Confederation
The signing of the Statute of Westminster
The founding of the United Nations
The end of the Second World War

quiz.q: In which Canadian city was Expo 67 held?
options: Toronto
Ottawa
Montreal
Vancouver

quiz.q: Approximately how many visitors did Expo 67 draw?
options: Exactly one thousand
Fewer than one hundred
Tens of millions
No visitors attended at all

quiz.q: What does Expo 67 often symbolize in accounts of Canadian history?
options: A time when Canada had no relations with other countries
A period of complete international isolation for Canada
The end of all international exhibitions in Canada
Canadian confidence and international engagement during the centennial era

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: English Review: Grammar, Reading, Writing, and Oral Communication (Days 171-179)
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand review: students revisit reported speech, the epilogue and denouement, the travel narrative, sports broadcasting commentary, the detective and mystery genre, nonverbal communication, film editing and montage, sentence combining, and the product review.

quiz.q: What does reported speech do?
options: Repeats a statement word for word inside quotation marks
Converts a sentence into a question with no other change
Removes all verbs from a sentence
Restates what someone said without using their exact words or quotation marks

quiz.q: What does the denouement of a narrative do?
options: Introduces the main conflict for the first time
Replaces the need for a climax entirely
Resolves remaining plot threads after the climax
Occurs before any characters are introduced

quiz.q: What does a travel narrative typically recount?
options: A scientific report with no narrative elements
A purely fictional world with no real setting
A single event that occurs entirely at home
A journey to an unfamiliar location

quiz.q: What does the detective and mystery genre typically centre on?
options: A story with no conflict or problem to solve
A purely descriptive account of a setting with no plot
A collection of unrelated poems with no narrative
Solving a crime or puzzle through the gathering of clues and logical deduction

quiz.q: What is montage?
options: A technique used only in silent films with no sound
A single unedited continuous shot with no cuts
An editing technique that assembles a rapid sequence of images
A method of removing all sound from a film entirely

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Math Review: Number Theory, Calculus, Algebra, and Statistics (Days 171-179)
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand review: students revisit the Sieve of Eratosthenes, the Mean Value Theorem, rational inequalities, Eulerian and Hamiltonian paths, the F-distribution and ANOVA, spherical geometry, the Rational Root Theorem, antiderivatives, and the law of large numbers.

quiz.q: What does the Sieve of Eratosthenes find?
options: All prime numbers up to a given limit
The sum of an arithmetic series
The area of a triangle
The exact square root of a number

quiz.q: What does the Mean Value Theorem guarantee for a smooth, continuous function over an interval?
options: That the function must be equal to zero somewhere in the interval
That the function has no derivative anywhere
That the interval must contain only whole numbers
At least one point where the instantaneous rate of change equals the average rate of change

quiz.q: What must an Eulerian path visit exactly once?
options: The exact midpoint of a graph
Every possible graph that could ever exist
Every edge of a graph
Every colour used to draw a graph

quiz.q: What does analysis of variance, or ANOVA, test?
options: Whether the means of three or more groups differ significantly
Whether a single number is prime
The exact slope of a straight line
The area under a single point on a graph

quiz.q: What is an antiderivative of a function?
options: A function that has no derivative at all
A new function whose derivative equals the original function
A function with no relationship to the original function
The exact same function written in a different colour

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Science Review: Physics, Chemistry, Earth Science, and Biology (Days 171-179)
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand review: students revisit light dispersion in rainbows, the chemistry of photography, sand dunes, the human liver, lenses and image formation, soap and saponification, deltas and river systems, the salmon run, and the chemistry of fermentation.

quiz.q: What natural event causes light to disperse into a rainbow?
options: Sunlight being absorbed entirely by the atmosphere
Moonlight reflecting off a still lake with no droplets present
Sunlight entering raindrops and being refracted and internally reflected
Sunlight passing through a completely opaque object

quiz.q: What type of compound makes traditional photographic film light-sensitive?
options: Pure carbon
Distilled water
Silver halide compounds
Table salt

quiz.q: What is one of the main functions of the liver?
options: Regulating body temperature directly through the skin
Filtering blood and breaking down toxins
Producing sound for the vocal cords
Pumping blood throughout the entire body

quiz.q: What chemical process produces soap?
options: Distillation
Saponification
Electrolysis
Combustion

quiz.q: What term describes the demanding migratory life cycle of salmon?
options: The hibernation cycle
The photosynthetic cycle
The predator cycle
The salmon run

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: History Review: The Diefenbaker-Pearson Era in Canada (Days 171-179)
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand review: students revisit the 1957 federal election, the Canadian Bill of Rights of 1960, the extension of the federal vote to Indigenous peoples, the nuclear weapons controversy, the 1963 election, the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism, the flag debate, youth activism, and Expo 67.

quiz.q: Which party won the 1957 federal election?
options: The Social Credit Party
The Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
The Progressive Conservatives, led by John Diefenbaker
The Liberals, led by Louis St. Laurent

quiz.q: In what year was the Canadian Bill of Rights introduced?
What did the federal government do in 1960 regarding First Nations peoples?
options: It ended all federal elections in Canada
It extended the federal vote to First Nations peoples living on reserves
It removed the right to vote from all Canadian citizens
It created an entirely new federal electoral system

quiz.q: What was the Great Flag Debate about?
options: Choosing a new national anthem
Selecting a new national capital city
Adopting a new national currency
Adopting a new, distinctly Canadian national flag

quiz.q: What milestone did Expo 67 help celebrate?
options: The founding of the United Nations
One hundred years since Canadian Confederation
The end of the Second World War
The signing of the Statute of Westminster

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Reading: Analyzing Flashback and Nonlinear Timelines
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: a flashback interrupts the chronological order of a narrative to show an earlier event, and writers use flashbacks and other nonlinear timelines to reveal backstory, build suspense, or highlight a connection between past and present without following strict chronological order.

quiz.q: What does a flashback do within a narrative?
options: Predicts an event that has not yet happened
Removes all characters from the story
Interrupts the chronological order to show an earlier event
Repeats the current scene word for word

quiz.q: What is one reason a writer might use a flashback?
options: To make the timeline impossible to follow
To end the story before it begins
To remove the need for a plot
To reveal backstory or build suspense

quiz.q: What term describes a narrative structure that does not follow strict chronological order?
options: A completely linear timeline
A single unbroken timeline with no gaps
A nonlinear timeline
A timeline with only future events

quiz.q: What might a flashback highlight about the relationship between past and present events?
options: That the two time periods are entirely unrelated
That the present has no bearing on the story
That the past can never influence a character
A meaningful connection between them

quiz.q: Why might a nonlinear timeline challenge a reader more than a strictly chronological one?
options: The reader must piece together the order of events rather than following them in sequence
Nonlinear timelines cannot include any flashback
Nonlinear timelines always confuse readers with no purpose
A nonlinear timeline removes every character from the plot

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Number Theory: Goldbachs Conjecture
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: Goldbachs Conjecture proposes that every even integer greater than two can be written as the sum of two prime numbers, a statement that has been verified for an enormous range of numbers through computation yet still has no formal mathematical proof.

quiz.q: What does Goldbachs Conjecture propose?
options: That no even number can ever be divided evenly
That every odd integer is automatically prime
That prime numbers do not exist beyond one hundred
That every even integer greater than two can be written as the sum of two prime numbers

quiz.q: What has happened to Goldbachs Conjecture despite extensive testing?
options: It has been completely disproven
It has never been tested for any number
It has been formally proven for all numbers
It has been verified for an enormous range of numbers but never formally proven

quiz.q: Which pair of primes could demonstrate Goldbachs Conjecture for the number 10?
options: 4 and 6
10 and 0
1 and 9
5 and 5, or 3 and 7

quiz.q: Why is Goldbachs Conjecture still considered a conjecture rather than a theorem?
options: No general mathematical proof covering all even numbers has yet been found
It applies only to negative numbers
It was proven true in the eighteenth century
It has already been proven false

quiz.q: What type of number does Goldbachs Conjecture say every even integer greater than two can be expressed as the sum of?
options: Two prime numbers
Two even numbers only
Two negative numbers
Two irrational numbers

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Physics: Terminal Velocity and Air Resistance
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand: terminal velocity is the constant maximum speed a falling object reaches once the upward force of air resistance grows large enough to balance the downward force of gravity, after which the object stops accelerating and falls at a steady rate.

quiz.q: What is terminal velocity?
options: The speed of an object with no air resistance acting on it
The constant maximum speed a falling object reaches when air resistance balances gravity
The speed at which an object accelerates forever without limit
The speed of an object the instant it is released

quiz.q: What happens to an objects acceleration once it reaches terminal velocity?
options: The acceleration increases without limit
The acceleration becomes zero and the object falls at a constant speed
The object instantly stops moving entirely
The object begins to move upward

quiz.q: What two forces balance each other at terminal velocity?
options: Gravity and air resistance
Electric force and gravity
Buoyancy and tension
Friction and magnetism

quiz.q: How does the surface area of a falling object affect its terminal velocity?
options: Terminal velocity depends only on colour, not surface area
A larger surface area always increases terminal velocity
Surface area has no effect on air resistance whatsoever
A larger surface area generally increases air resistance and lowers terminal velocity

quiz.q: Why does a skydiver reach a slower terminal velocity when their parachute opens?
options: The parachute greatly increases air resistance acting against gravity
The parachute increases the skydivers mass
The parachute removes gravity entirely
The parachute eliminates all air resistance

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: Trudeaumania and the 1968 Federal Election
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: Trudeaumania describes the wave of enthusiasm surrounding Pierre Trudeau during the 1968 federal election, which the Liberals won decisively behind his charisma, media appeal, and vision of a Just Society, ushering in a new era of Canadian federal politics.

quiz.q: What does the term Trudeaumania describe?
options: A federal law passed in 1968
The wave of public enthusiasm surrounding Pierre Trudeau during the 1968 election
A treaty signed between Canada and France
A new Canadian currency introduced in 1968

quiz.q: Which party won the 1968 federal election?
options: The Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
The Progressive Conservatives, led by John Diefenbaker
The Liberal Party, led by Pierre Trudeau
The Social Credit Party

quiz.q: What personal qualities were often credited with fueling Trudeaumania?
options: A total avoidance of public appearances
Charisma and strong media appeal
An exclusively written campaign with no public events
A complete lack of any political vision

quiz.q: What vision did Trudeau associate with his political platform around this period?
options: The Meech Lake Accord
The National Policy
The Just Society
The White Paper

quiz.q: What broader shift did the 1968 election help usher in for Canadian federal politics?
options: A return to nineteenth-century political parties
A new era shaped by Trudeaus leadership and political style
The abolition of federal elections
The permanent end of the Liberal Party

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Writing: The Letter to the Editor
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: a letter to the editor is a piece of persuasive writing submitted to a newspaper or publication in response to a current issue or a previously published article, using a clear argument, supporting evidence, and a respectful but urgent tone to influence public opinion.

quiz.q: What is a letter to the editor?
options: A piece of persuasive writing submitted to a newspaper or publication in response to a current issue
A recipe published in a cooking magazine
A private letter never intended for publication
A weather report with no argument

quiz.q: What tone does an effective letter to the editor typically use?
options: A tone that avoids addressing the issue
A tone with no clear opinion at all
A respectful but urgent tone
An entirely comedic tone with no argument

quiz.q: What might a letter to the editor respond to?
options: A private conversation with no public relevance
A current issue or a previously published article
A recipe with no argument
A math equation with no connection to current events

quiz.q: What helps make a letter to the editor persuasive?
options: Ignoring the topic entirely
A clear argument supported by evidence
Random unrelated facts with no connection to the issue
A complete absence of any opinion

quiz.q: Why might a reader write a letter to the editor rather than simply discussing an issue privately?
options: To influence public opinion by reaching a wider audience through publication
To avoid taking any position on the issue
Because letters to the editor are never read by anyone
Because private discussion always reaches more people

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Calculus: Linear Approximation and Differentials
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: linear approximation uses the tangent line at a known point on a function to estimate the value of the function at a nearby point, with the differential representing the small change in the linear approximation that corresponds to a small change in the input.

quiz.q: What does linear approximation use to estimate a functions value near a known point?
options: The area under the entire curve
The tangent line at that known point
A completely unrelated function
A random guess with no mathematical basis

quiz.q: What does the differential represent in linear approximation?
options: The small change in the linear approximation corresponding to a small change in input
The maximum value a function can ever reach
The total area under the curve
The exact value of the function at every point

quiz.q: Why is linear approximation generally most accurate close to the known point?
options: Tangent lines are always identical to the curve everywhere
Linear approximation ignores the shape of the curve entirely
The tangent line closely matches the curve only near the point of tangency
Linear approximation is equally accurate at any distance from the point

quiz.q: What information is needed to construct a linear approximation of a function at a point?
options: Only the y-intercept of the graph
The function value and its derivative at that point
The area under the curve across its entire domain
The second derivative at every point on the curve

quiz.q: In what type of real-world situation might linear approximation be useful?
options: Measuring a quantity with no relationship to calculus
Estimating a small change in output resulting from a small change in input
Finding the colour of a graphed function
Calculating the exact value of a function infinitely far from a known point

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Chemistry: Food Preservation and the Chemistry of Spoilage
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand: food spoilage occurs when microorganisms and chemical reactions such as oxidation break down the compounds in food, and preservation methods including refrigeration, drying, canning, and the addition of salt or acid work by slowing microbial growth or altering the chemical conditions food needs to spoil.

quiz.q: What commonly causes food spoilage?
options: Microorganisms and chemical reactions such as oxidation
A complete absence of any chemical activity
Food becoming instantly sterile with no further change
The total removal of all bacteria with no other cause

quiz.q: How does refrigeration help preserve food?
options: It has no effect on microorganisms at all
It instantly destroys all chemical reactions in food
It increases the rate of microbial growth
It slows the growth rate of microorganisms that cause spoilage

quiz.q: How can adding salt help preserve food?
options: It draws water out of microbial cells, slowing their growth
It has no chemical effect on food
It removes all nutrients from the food
It always speeds up spoilage

quiz.q: What role can acid play in food preservation, such as in pickling?
options: It has no effect on the growth of microorganisms
It removes the need for any other preservation method
It creates conditions that many spoilage microorganisms cannot easily survive in
It always accelerates spoilage

quiz.q: Why does drying food help prevent spoilage?
options: Removing moisture limits the water microorganisms need to grow
Drying has no effect on microbial growth
Microorganisms grow faster in dry conditions than in moist ones
Drying always increases the moisture content of food

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: The Just Society: Trudeaus Political Vision
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: the Just Society was the guiding political vision Pierre Trudeau promoted throughout his early years as prime minister, emphasizing individual rights, bilingualism, and greater social and economic equality as central goals for federal policy in Canada.

quiz.q: What was the Just Society?
options: A new Canadian province
The guiding political vision Pierre Trudeau promoted as prime minister
A federal department created in 1968
A treaty signed between Canada and Britain

quiz.q: Which values did the Just Society emphasize?
options: A return to nineteenth-century policies
Individual rights, bilingualism, and greater social and economic equality
The abolition of all federal programs
Complete isolation from international affairs

quiz.q: Who is most closely associated with promoting the idea of the Just Society?
options: Louis St. Laurent
Pierre Trudeau
Lester Pearson
John Diefenbaker

quiz.q: During which period did the Just Society serve as a guiding political vision?
options: Trudeaus early years as prime minister, beginning in the late 1960s
The 1867-1900 period of Canadian settlement
The Second World War
The 1867 Confederation debates

quiz.q: How did the Just Society relate to federal policy goals of the period?
options: It focused exclusively on foreign trade agreements
It set out central goals for federal policy such as expanding rights and equality
It had no connection to any federal policy
It called for the complete elimination of federal government

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Grammar: Split Infinitives and Usage Debates
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: a split infinitive occurs when a word, usually an adverb, is placed between the word to and the verb that follows it, as in to boldly go, a construction once widely considered incorrect but now generally accepted in modern usage when it improves clarity or emphasis.

quiz.q: What is a split infinitive?
options: A verb with two different subjects
A sentence that begins with a question word
A sentence with no verb at all
A construction where a word is placed between to and the verb that follows it

quiz.q: Which of the following is an example of a split infinitive?
options: Going to boldly
To go boldly forward
Boldly to go now
To boldly go

quiz.q: How was the split infinitive traditionally viewed by many grammar guides?
options: As a construction found only in poetry
As an incorrect or awkward construction to be avoided
As a rule with no historical basis whatsoever
As the only correct way to form an infinitive

quiz.q: How is the split infinitive generally viewed in modern usage?
options: As generally acceptable, especially when it improves clarity or emphasis
As always grammatically incorrect with no exception
As acceptable only in legal documents
As a construction that no longer exists in English

quiz.q: Why might a writer choose to split an infinitive deliberately?
options: Because English grammar requires every infinitive to be split
To make a sentence impossible to understand
Because split infinitives always weaken a sentence
To place emphasis on the adverb or to avoid an awkward sentence structure

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Geometry: Loci and Locus Problems
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: a locus is the set of all points that satisfy a given geometric condition, such as a fixed distance from a point or an equal distance from two points, and locus problems ask students to describe or sketch the shape formed by all such points.

quiz.q: What is a locus in geometry?
options: A single fixed point with no other points nearby
A line with an undefined length
The set of all points that satisfy a given geometric condition
A shape with no defined boundary at all

quiz.q: What shape is formed by the locus of points a fixed distance from a single given point?
options: A circle
A square
A straight line
A single point

quiz.q: What shape is formed by the locus of points equidistant from two fixed points?
options: A single point exactly halfway between them with no other points included
The perpendicular bisector of the segment joining the two points
A triangle connecting the two points
A circle centred on one of the two points

quiz.q: What does a locus problem typically ask a student to do?
options: Solve an equation with no geometric meaning
Describe or sketch the shape formed by all points satisfying a given condition
Calculate the exact area of an unrelated triangle
List every integer between two numbers

quiz.q: Which real-world application might rely on locus reasoning?
options: Calculating the derivative of a polynomial function
Determining the safe zone equidistant from two transmission towers
Converting a decimal to a percentage
Balancing a chemical equation

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Earth Science: Tides and the Physics of Ocean Tides
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand: ocean tides are the periodic rise and fall of sea level caused primarily by the gravitational pull of the moon and, to a lesser extent, the sun, producing predictable high and low tide cycles that vary with the relative positions of the Earth, moon, and sun.

quiz.q: What primarily causes ocean tides?
options: The gravitational pull of the moon and, to a lesser extent, the sun
Volcanic activity beneath the ocean floor
Wind blowing across the surface of the ocean
Changes in ocean water temperature alone

quiz.q: What pattern do ocean tides generally follow?
options: A pattern that never repeats
A predictable periodic rise and fall of sea level
A completely random and unpredictable pattern
A single rise with no corresponding fall

quiz.q: What produces especially strong tides known as spring tides?
options: The complete absence of any gravitational pull
An alignment of the sun, Earth, and moon that combines their gravitational effects
The arrival of the spring season each year
A sudden drop in ocean temperature

quiz.q: What term describes the weaker tides that occur when the sun and moon are at right angles relative to Earth?
options: Neap tides
Spring tides
Storm tides
King tides

quiz.q: Why is the moons gravitational pull more influential on tides than the suns, despite the suns much greater mass?
options: The moon is more massive than the sun
Distance has no effect on gravitational influence
The sun has no gravitational pull at all
The moon is far closer to Earth, which increases its tidal influence

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: Canadas Adoption of the Metric System in the 1970s
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: in the 1970s the federal government began converting Canada from imperial to metric measurement in weather reporting, road signs, and consumer goods, a gradual process intended to align Canadian trade and daily life with the metric standard used by most of the world.

quiz.q: What change did the federal government begin implementing in the 1970s?
options: Ending federal elections
Abolishing all provincial governments
Replacing the Canadian dollar with a new currency
Converting Canada from imperial to metric measurement

quiz.q: In which areas of daily life was the metric conversion first introduced?
options: Only in federal court proceedings
Weather reporting, road signs, and consumer goods
Only in international treaties
Only in scientific laboratories with no public application

quiz.q: Why did the federal government pursue metric conversion?
options: To align Canadian trade and daily life with the metric standard used by most of the world
To make measurement more difficult for Canadians
To eliminate the need for any measurement system
To copy a system used only by one other country

quiz.q: How would the transition to the metric system in Canada best be described?
options: A gradual process introduced over time
A change reversed within one year
A process that was never actually implemented
An instantaneous change completed in a single day

quiz.q: What measurement system did Canada primarily use before the metric conversion?
options: No standardized measurement system at all
The imperial system
The metric system
A system unique to Canada with no international counterpart

subjects.subject: English
subjects.title: Media Literacy: Analyzing Documentary Film Techniques
subjects.summary: Grade 10 English strand: documentary filmmakers use techniques such as archival footage, expert interviews, voice-over narration, and selective editing to present factual subject matter persuasively, meaning viewers must think critically about whose perspective a documentary emphasizes and what it leaves out.

quiz.q: Which technique might a documentary filmmaker use to present factual subject matter?
options: A completely fictional plot with no factual basis
An animated sequence with no connection to reality
A script written entirely in verse
Archival footage, expert interviews, and voice-over narration

quiz.q: Why might a viewer need to think critically when watching a documentary?
options: Documentary filmmakers cannot select which footage to include
Documentaries never involve any editing choices
Documentaries always present every possible perspective equally
Documentaries can emphasize a particular perspective and leave out other information

quiz.q: What is the purpose of voice-over narration in many documentaries?
options: To replace every visual image with silence
To remove all information from the film
To guide viewers through the subject matter and provide context
To prevent the audience from understanding the topic

quiz.q: How can selective editing shape a viewers understanding of a documentary subject?
options: Editing only affects the length of a film, not its meaning
Selective editing always presents a fully neutral account
By determining which footage and interviews are included or left out
Editing has no effect on how a documentary is understood

quiz.q: Why might expert interviews be included in a documentary?
options: To confuse viewers with unrelated information
To lend credibility and provide informed perspective on the subject
To remove any factual basis from the film
Because documentaries are required to include no spoken interviews

subjects.subject: Math
subjects.title: Algebra: Solving Systems Using Matrices and Gaussian Elimination
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Math strand: a system of linear equations can be represented as a matrix, and Gaussian elimination is a systematic method of using row operations to transform that matrix into a simpler form from which the solution to the system can be read directly.

quiz.q: How can a system of linear equations be represented for use with Gaussian elimination?
options: As a single word problem with no numerical structure
As a circle graph
As a single unrelated number
As a matrix

quiz.q: What is Gaussian elimination?
options: A method with no connection to systems of equations
A method for graphing a single point
A systematic method of using row operations to simplify a matrix and solve a system
A method for finding the area of a triangle

quiz.q: What is the goal of applying row operations during Gaussian elimination?
options: To transform the matrix into a simpler form from which the solution can be read
To convert the matrix into a single unrelated equation
To remove all numbers from the matrix
To make the matrix impossible to solve

quiz.q: Which of the following is an example of a row operation used in Gaussian elimination?
options: Deleting every row from the matrix
Replacing all numbers in the matrix with zero
Adding a multiple of one row to another row
Converting the matrix into a word problem

quiz.q: Why is Gaussian elimination useful for systems with more than two variables?
options: It only works for systems with exactly one variable
It eliminates the need to ever solve for a variable
It cannot be applied to any system with more than one equation
It provides an organized, systematic approach that scales to larger systems

subjects.subject: Science
subjects.title: Biology: Decomposers and Nutrient Cycling in Ecosystems
subjects.summary: Grade 10 Science strand: decomposers such as fungi and bacteria break down dead organisms and waste material into simpler substances, releasing nutrients back into the soil and water so they can be reused by other living things, making decomposers essential to nutrient cycling within an ecosystem.

quiz.q: What role do decomposers play in an ecosystem?
options: They produce all of the oxygen in an ecosystem
They consume only living plants and animals
They break down dead organisms and waste into simpler substances
They prevent any nutrients from returning to the soil

quiz.q: Which organisms are common examples of decomposers?
options: Fungi and bacteria
Only birds of prey
Only photosynthetic plants
Only large mammals

quiz.q: What happens to nutrients once decomposers break down dead material?
options: They are converted directly into oxygen gas
They are released back into the soil and water for reuse
They are permanently destroyed and lost from the ecosystem
They remain locked inside the decomposer forever

quiz.q: Why are decomposers considered essential to nutrient cycling?
options: They allow nutrients from dead organisms to be reused by other living things
They have no effect on the availability of nutrients
They only cycle nutrients within their own bodies
They remove all nutrients from an ecosystem permanently

quiz.q: What might happen to an ecosystem if decomposers were removed entirely?
options: All nutrients would instantly double in quantity
Every organism in the ecosystem would immediately become a decomposer
Dead material would accumulate and nutrients would not be efficiently recycled
Nothing would change in the ecosystem

subjects.subject: History
subjects.title: The Immigration Act of 1976 and the Points System
subjects.summary: Grade 10 History strand: the Immigration Act of 1976 established a legal framework that formalized the points system for evaluating prospective immigrants based on factors such as education, skills, and language ability, shaping Canadian immigration policy on the basis of qualifications rather than national origin.

quiz.q: What did the Immigration Act of 1976 establish?
options: A ban on all immigration to Canada
A new provincial border
A legal framework that formalized the points system for evaluating prospective immigrants
